questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.00620 is
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; 6, 2 and the trailing 0 are significant, giving 3 significant figures.
questions.trick: Leading zeros never count; only 6, 2 and the trailing 0 are significant.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Molarity is expressed in mol per kg of solvent
Molality does not change with temperature
1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP
questions.explanation: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, not per kg of solvent — that is the definition of molality.
questions.trick: Molarity is always per litre of solution, never per kg of solvent.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of atoms present in 0.5 mol of N$_2$ gas is
questions.explanation: 0.5 mol N$_2$ = 1 mol N atoms = $6.022\times10^{23}$ atoms.
questions.trick: Atoms = moles × atomicity × $N_A$; N$_2$ is diatomic.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following numbers has exactly three significant figures?
questions.explanation: 2.50 has three significant figures (2, 5, 0); leading zeros in 0.025 and 0.0025 are not significant.
questions.trick: A trailing zero after the decimal point counts as significant.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A mixture contains 4.4 g of CO$_2$ and 2.8 g of N$_2$. The total number of molecules present in the mixture is
questions.trick: Find moles of each species separately, add them, then × $N_A$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A sample of impure CaCO$_3$ (80% pure) weighing 12.5 g is heated completely as $\text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$. The mass of CO$_2$ released is (Ca = 40)
questions.explanation: Pure CaCO$_3 = 0.80\times12.5 = 10$ g $= 0.1$ mol, giving $0.1$ mol CO$_2 = 4.4$ g.
questions.trick: Use only the pure fraction (purity% × mass) before converting to moles.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which subshell is filled immediately after 4s according to the Aufbau principle?
questions.explanation: Using $(n+l)$ values, 3d ($n+l=5$) has lower energy than 4p ($n+l=5$ but higher $n$) is filled right after 4s in the Aufbau order 1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d...
questions.trick: Aufbau order by $(n+l)$: after 4s comes 3d, not 4p.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The energy of an electron in the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen is
questions.trick: $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV; just substitute $n=2$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of angular nodes in a d orbital is
questions.explanation: Angular nodes $= l = 2$ for a d orbital ($l=2$).
questions.trick: Angular nodes $= l$; for d orbital, $l=2$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The energy required to excite an electron in a hydrogen atom from $n=1$ to $n=2$ is
questions.trick: $\Delta E = E_2-E_1$; excitation energy is always a positive difference.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: An orbital with $n = 4, l = 2$ is designated as
questions.explanation: $l = 0,1,2,3$ correspond to s, p, d, f respectively; so $l=2$ with $n=4$ is 4d.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The frequency of a photon having energy $3.03\times10^{-19}$ J is (h = $6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s)
questions.trick: $\nu = E/h$ — direct substitution, no unit traps.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of increasing first ionisation enthalpy for P, S, Cl and Ar is
questions.explanation: S dips below P because P's half-filled 3p$^3$ is extra stable (like N vs O), so the actual order is S < P < Cl < Ar, not the naively expected monotonic increase.
questions.trick: Half-filled 3p$^3$ in P is extra stable → S dips below P in IE.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The drop in ionisation enthalpy on going from group 2 to group 13 across a period (e.g. Mg to Al) is mainly due to
options: extra shielding provided by inner d-electrons
the added electron entering a p-orbital, which is less penetrating and more easily removed than an s-electron
a sharp increase in atomic size
a sudden decrease in nuclear charge
questions.explanation: The outermost electron in group 13 elements occupies a p-orbital, which is shielded by the filled s-orbital and is easier to remove than an s-electron, lowering ionisation enthalpy relative to group 2.
questions.trick: New p-electron is more shielded/penetrates less than s → IE drops at group 13.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Noble gases have very high ionisation enthalpies because
options: they have small atomic size only
they have completely filled stable electronic configurations
questions.explanation: A fully-filled octet ($ns^2np^6$) is extremely stable, so removing an electron requires very high energy.
questions.trick: Fully-filled octet ($ns^2np^6$) resists electron removal → highest IE in period.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Among Na, Mg, Al and Si, the element with the highest first ionisation enthalpy is
questions.explanation: Actual IE$_1$ values (kJ mol$^{-1}$): Na 496, Al 578, Mg 738, Si 786. Despite the Mg–Al dip, Si (further right, with an increasing effective nuclear charge) has the highest IE$_1$ of this set.
questions.trick: Don't assume smooth trend across group 2–13; check actual IE values when unsure.
questions.tip: Don't assume the period trend is perfectly monotonic across group boundaries — check actual anomalies at groups 2→13 and 15→16.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Regarding electron gain enthalpy of oxygen and sulphur, which statement is correct?
options: S has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than O
neither has a negative electron gain enthalpy
O has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than S
questions.explanation: Like F vs Cl, the smaller O atom has greater electron-electron repulsion when gaining an electron, so S (larger, less repulsion) has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than O.
questions.trick: Smaller atom → more e–e repulsion on gaining e– → O less negative than S.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The lanthanoid elements are placed in period
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, Z=58–71) belong to period 6, following La.
questions.trick: Lanthanoids (Z=58–71) sit in period 6, right after La.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene has a net dipole moment, unlike its trans isomer, because
options: the two C–Cl bond dipoles do not cancel due to the cis arrangement
the two C–Cl bond dipoles cancel completely
questions.explanation: In the cis isomer, both C–Cl bonds point to the same side, so their dipole moment vectors add up instead of cancelling as they do in the symmetric trans isomer.
questions.trick: Same-side (cis) bond dipoles add up instead of cancelling like in trans.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The hybridisation and shape of NH$_4^+$ ion are
questions.explanation: N has 4 bond pairs (3 N–H + 1 coordinate bond to H$^+$) and no lone pair, giving sp$^3$ hybridisation and a regular tetrahedral shape.
questions.trick: 4 bond pairs (incl. coordinate bond), no lone pair → sp$^3$, tetrahedral.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of increasing bond order among He$_2$, B$_2$, O$_2$ and N$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Bond orders: He$_2$ = 0, B$_2$ = 1, O$_2$ = 2, N$_2$ = 3, giving the increasing order He$_2$ < B$_2$ < O$_2$ < N$_2$.
questions.trick: Recall bond orders directly: He$_2$=0, B$_2$=1, O$_2$=2, N$_2$=3.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The shape of SF$_4$ molecule is
questions.explanation: S has 4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (sp$^3$d, AB$_4$E type). The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, giving a see-saw shape.
questions.trick: AB$_4$E (sp$^3$d), lone pair equatorial → see-saw shape.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of decreasing carbon–carbon bond length is
questions.explanation: More shared electron pairs pull the bonded atoms closer together, so bond length decreases as bond order increases: single > double > triple.
questions.trick: More bonding pairs pull atoms closer → bond length falls as bond order rises.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following molecules has the largest dipole moment?
questions.explanation: BF$_3$ and CH$_4$ are symmetric (zero). In NH$_3$ the lone-pair moment and N–H moments point the same way; in NF$_3$ they oppose, so NH$_3$ (1.47 D) > NF$_3$ (0.23 D).
questions.trick: Lone-pair moment adds to bond moments in NH$_3$ but opposes them in NF$_3$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In ozone (O$_3$), the two O–O bond lengths are equal because of
questions.explanation: O$_3$ is a resonance hybrid of two structures; each bond has partial double-bond character (bond length 128 pm, between 121 and 148 pm).
questions.trick: Equal, intermediate bond lengths signal resonance, not a fixed single/double bond.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT isoelectronic with N$_2$?
questions.explanation: N$_2$, CO, CN$^-$ and NO$^+$ all have 14 electrons and bond order 3. O$_2$ has 16 electrons.
questions.trick: Isoelectronic with N$_2$ means 14 electrons; O$_2$ has 16, so it's the odd one out.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of sigma and pi bonds in HCN (H–C≡N) are respectively
questions.explanation: H–C is 1 σ bond; C≡N (triple bond) is 1 σ + 2 π bonds. Total: 2 σ and 2 π bonds.
questions.trick: Each bond contributes 1 $\sigma$; a triple bond adds 2 $\pi$ on top.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The bond order of O$_2^-$ (superoxide ion) is
questions.explanation: O$_2$ has bond order 2 (10 bonding, 6 antibonding). Adding one electron to $\pi^*$ gives $(10-7)/2 = 1.5$.
questions.trick: For BO use $(N_b-N_a)/2$; O$_2^-$ adds one antibonding electron to O$_2$'s BO 2.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The shape of SF$_6$ molecule is
questions.explanation: S has 6 bond pairs, no lone pairs: sp$^3$d$^2$, octahedral, bond angle 90°.
questions.trick: 6 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → sp$^3$d$^2$, octahedral — straight from VSEPR count.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The hybridisation of Xe in XeF$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Xe has 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs, requiring 5 electron domains, i.e. sp$^3$d hybridisation (linear AB$_2$E$_3$ shape).
questions.trick: 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs = 5 domains → sp$^3$d, linear shape.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A central atom shows a bond angle of 109.5° with no lone pairs on it. Its hybridisation is
questions.explanation: A perfect tetrahedral bond angle of 109.5° with four bond pairs and no lone pairs corresponds to sp$^3$ hybridisation.
questions.trick: 109.5° with zero lone pairs is the sp$^3$ tetrahedral signature angle.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly from 10 L to 20 L at 300 K. The work done (w, IUPAC convention) is ($R = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -1\times8.314\times300\times\ln2 = -8.314\times300\times0.693 \approx -1729$ J.
questions.trick: $w=-nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$ for isothermal reversible expansion — plug in directly.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Using bond enthalpies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431 kJ mol$^{-1}$, the enthalpy change for $H_2(g) + Cl_2(g) \to 2HCl(g)$ is
questions.explanation: $\Delta H = \Sigma BE_{reactants} - \Sigma BE_{products} = (436+242) - 2(431) = 678 - 862 = -184$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $\Delta H = \Sigma BE_{reactants} - \Sigma BE_{products}$ — bonds broken minus bonds formed.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid with a strong base is
options: about $-57.3$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, nearly the same for all strong acid–strong base pairs
questions.explanation: Since strong acids and bases are fully ionised, neutralisation is essentially $H^+ + OH^- \to H_2O$ in every case, releasing about 57.3 kJ per mole of water formed.
questions.trick: Strong acid + strong base = net $H^++OH^-\to H_2O$ → always $\approx-57.3$ kJ/mol.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Hess's law is a direct consequence of the fact that
questions.explanation: Since $H$ depends only on initial and final states, the total $\Delta H$ for a reaction is the same regardless of the number of steps taken.
questions.trick: Hess's law works because $H$ is a state function, so paths don't matter.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: All naturally occurring spontaneous processes are thermodynamically
questions.explanation: A truly reversible process is an idealised, infinitely slow limit; all real (spontaneous) processes occurring at a finite rate are irreversible.
questions.trick: Real, finite-rate spontaneous processes are always irreversible in practice.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Given: $C(s) + O_2(g) \to CO_2(g)$, $\Delta H = -393.5\,\text{kJ}$ and $CO(g) + \tfrac12O_2(g) \to CO_2(g)$, $\Delta H = -283.0\,\text{kJ}$. The enthalpy of formation of CO(g) is
questions.explanation: $\Delta H_f(CO) = \Delta H_1 - \Delta H_2 = -393.5 - (-283.0) = -110.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (subtracting the second equation from the first).
questions.trick: Subtract/add given equations so unwanted species cancel to give the target reaction.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A system that can exchange only energy, but not matter, with its surroundings is called a(n)
questions.explanation: A closed system allows energy transfer across its boundary but not matter transfer (e.g. a sealed, conducting container).
questions.trick: Closed system: energy crosses the boundary, matter does not.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is a state function?
questions.explanation: Enthalpy $H$ depends only on the initial and final states, unlike heat and work, which depend on the path taken.
questions.trick: State function depends only on start/end — heat and work are path functions.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A reaction has $\Delta H = -50\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S = -100\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$. It is spontaneous
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$; with $\Delta H<0$ and $\Delta S<0$, $\Delta G$ stays negative only while $T$ is small enough that $T\Delta S$ doesn't outweigh $\Delta H$: spontaneous at low $T$.
questions.trick: $-,-$ row of the sign table: spontaneous only at low $T$ (small $T\Delta S$).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a spontaneous process, the second law of thermodynamics requires that
questions.explanation: A spontaneous process increases the total entropy of the universe (system + surroundings), even if the system's own entropy decreases.
questions.trick: 2nd law needs $\Delta S_{universe}>0$, not necessarily the system alone.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: If $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$ for a reaction, it will be spontaneous
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ becomes negative only when $T$ is large enough that $T\Delta S$ exceeds $\Delta H$: spontaneous at high $T$.
questions.trick: $+,+$ row of sign table: spontaneous only at high $T$ ($T\Delta S$ dominates).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a process occurring at constant volume,
options: $q_v = \Delta U$, since no p-V work is done at constant volume
questions.explanation: At constant volume, $\Delta V = 0$ so $w = -p\Delta V = 0$, and from the first law $\Delta U = q_v + w = q_v$.
questions.trick: At constant volume, $w=0$, so $q_v=\Delta U$ exactly.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: According to the third law of thermodynamics, the entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance at 0 K is
questions.explanation: At 0 K a perfect crystal has only one possible microstate (perfect order), so its entropy is taken as zero.
questions.trick: Third law: perfect crystal at 0 K has one microstate → entropy = zero.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The molar solubility of AgCl in water, given $K_{sp} = 1.8\times10^{-10}$, is
questions.explanation: $K_{sp} = s^2 \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}$ M.
questions.trick: 1:1 salt: $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}$ — simple square root, no factors needed.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A 0.01 M solution of NH$_4$OH has $K_b = 1\times10^{-6}$. Its pH is approximately
questions.trick: $[OH^-]=\sqrt{K_bC}$ for a weak base; convert $pOH$ to $pH$ via 14 minus.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For $H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)$, $K_c = 50$. At an instant, $[H_2]=[I_2]=0.1$ M and $[HI]=0.4$ M. The reaction will proceed
options: the system is already at equilibrium
questions.explanation: $Q_c = (0.4)^2/(0.1\times0.1) = 16$, which is less than $K_c = 50$, so the reaction proceeds forward to form more HI until $Q_c = K_c$.
questions.trick: Compute $Q_c$ from given concentrations, compare to $K_c$ to find direction.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For $PCl_5(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g)$, $K_c = 1.8$ at 500 K. The value of $K_p$ is (R = 0.0821 L atm K$^{-1}$mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\Delta n_g = 2-1 = 1$; $K_p = K_c(RT)^1 = 1.8\times0.0821\times500 \approx 73.9$.
questions.trick: $K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$; here $\Delta n_g=1$, so multiply by $RT$ once.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The pH of a $10^{-3}$ M HCl solution is
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid, fully dissociated: $[H^+] = 10^{-3}$ M, so $pH = -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$.
questions.trick: Strong acid fully dissociates: $pH = -\log[H^+]$ directly from concentration.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For an endothermic reaction, increasing the temperature causes the equilibrium constant $K$ to
questions.explanation: Raising temperature favours the endothermic (heat-absorbing) direction; since the forward reaction is endothermic here, more products form, increasing $K$.
questions.trick: Endothermic forward reaction: heating increases $K$, favouring products.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The solubility of AgCl ($K_{sp} = 1.8\times10^{-10}$) in 0.1 M NaCl solution is approximately
questions.explanation: With a common ion, $[Cl^-] \approx 0.1$ M (from NaCl); $s = K_{sp}/[Cl^-] = 1.8\times10^{-10}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}$ M — much lower solubility than in pure water (common ion effect).
questions.trick: Common ion effect: $s \approx K_{sp}/[\text{common ion}]$, not $\sqrt{K_{sp}}$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Common ion effect on the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt
options: converts it to a strong electrolyte
questions.explanation: Adding a common ion shifts the dissolution equilibrium backward (Le Chatelier), decreasing solubility, e.g. adding NaCl decreases AgCl solubility.
questions.trick: Common ion pushes dissolution equilibrium backward — solubility always drops.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: If $K_a$ of an acid is $10^{-5}$, its $pK_a$ and conjugate base's $pK_b$ are
questions.explanation: $pK_a = -\log(10^{-5}) = 5$. Since $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ for a conjugate pair, $pK_b = 14 - 5 = 9$.
questions.trick: $pK_a+pK_b=14$ for a conjugate pair; compute $pK_a$ first, subtract from 14.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A 0.01 M solution of a weak acid HA has $K_a = 1\times10^{-6}$. Its pH is approximately
questions.trick: $[H^+]=\sqrt{K_aC}$ for a weak acid — plug in and take $-\log$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The equilibrium constant $K$ of a reaction changes only with a change in
questions.explanation: $K$ depends only on temperature; catalysts, concentration and pressure changes shift the position of equilibrium but leave $K$ unchanged at a given $T$.
questions.trick: $K$ changes with temperature only — catalyst/pressure/concentration never touch it.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Addition of a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium
options: does not shift equilibrium, only speeds up attaining it
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions equally, helping equilibrium to be reached faster without changing its position or $K$.
questions.trick: Catalyst speeds both directions equally — no shift, no change in $K$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: If the ionic product of a sparingly soluble salt in solution exceeds its $K_{sp}$,
questions.explanation: When the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$, the solution is supersaturated, and excess solid precipitates out until the ionic product equals $K_{sp}$.
questions.trick: Ionic product $> K_{sp}$ means supersaturated → excess solid precipitates.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: An acidic buffer solution can be prepared by mixing
questions.explanation: A weak acid (CH$_3$COOH) with its salt of a strong base (CH$_3$COONa) forms an acidic buffer. NH$_4$OH+NH$_4$Cl is a basic buffer.
questions.trick: Weak acid + its salt of a strong base = classic acidic buffer.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Adding solid CH$_3$COONa to a CH$_3$COOH solution
options: increases the degree of ionisation of CH$_3$COOH
has no effect on the degree of ionisation
decreases the degree of ionisation of CH$_3$COOH (common ion effect)
questions.explanation: The acetate ion from CH$_3$COONa is common to the acid's dissociation equilibrium; by Le Chatelier's principle it suppresses further ionisation of CH$_3$COOH.
questions.trick: Adding the salt's common ion suppresses the weak acid's own ionisation.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a reaction at a given instant, if the reaction quotient $Q$ is greater than $K_c$, the reaction will proceed
questions.explanation: When $Q > K$, there is a relative excess of products, so the reaction shifts in the reverse direction until $Q$ decreases to equal $K$.
questions.trick: $Q>K$ means excess product → reaction runs backward to catch up.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: If the solubility of AgCl is $s$ mol L$^{-1}$, its $K_{sp}$ is
questions.explanation: AgCl $\rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Cl^-$; $[Ag^+]=[Cl^-]=s$, so $K_{sp} = s\times s = s^2$.
questions.trick: 1:1 salt: $K_{sp}=s^2$ when both ions come from one formula unit.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following species is amphiprotic (can act as both a Bronsted acid and base)?
questions.explanation: HCO$_3^-$ can donate a proton (to form CO$_3^{2-}$) or accept one (to form H$_2$CO$_3$), so it is amphiprotic.
questions.trick: Amphiprotic species can both gain and lose a proton — look for an -HCO$_3^-$-type ion.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: On diluting a weak acid solution 100 times, its degree of dissociation ($\alpha$)
questions.explanation: By Ostwald's dilution law, $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$, so $\alpha \propto 1/\sqrt{C}$; diluting 100 times increases $\alpha$ by a factor of $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
questions.trick: $\alpha \propto 1/\sqrt{C}$; diluting 100$\times$ raises $\alpha$ by $\sqrt{100}=10\times$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The oxidation number of Fe in K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] is
questions.explanation: K$_4$ contributes +4, so the complex ion [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{4-}$ has charge -4. CN$^-$ contributes -6, so Fe $= -4-(-6) = +2$.
questions.trick: Balance outside the bracket first (K$_4$ = +4) to find the complex ion's charge, then solve inside.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which pair correctly represents an oxidant and its corresponding reductant in the same reaction $MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \to Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$?
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +2 (gains electrons, reduced, so MnO$_4^-$ is the oxidising agent); Fe goes from +2 to +3 (loses electron, oxidised, reducing agent).
questions.trick: The species that gets reduced (gains e$^-$) is the oxidant; the one oxidised is the reductant.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The oxidation number of oxygen in OF$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Since fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, O takes a positive oxidation number here: F(-1)×2 + O = 0 → O = +2, an exception to the usual -2.
questions.trick: F beats O in electronegativity → O flips to $+2$ in OF$_2$, an exception.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The reaction $2H_2O_2 \to 2H_2O + O_2$ is an example of a
questions.explanation: Oxygen in H$_2$O$_2$ (-1) is simultaneously reduced to -2 (in H$_2$O) and oxidised to 0 (in O$_2$), so the same element is both oxidised and reduced — disproportionation.
questions.trick: Same O atom split into higher and lower oxidation states → disproportionation again.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The equivalent weight of H$_2$O$_2$ (M = 34) when it acts as an oxidising agent (n-factor = 2) is
questions.explanation: As an oxidiser, O in H$_2$O$_2$ goes from -1 to -2, a gain of 2 electrons per molecule; equivalent weight $= 34/2 = 17$.
questions.trick: As oxidiser, H$_2$O$_2$'s O drops from $-1$ to $-2$ (gains 2e$^-$); eq. wt = M/2.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The average oxidation number of iron in Fe$_3$O$_4$ (a mixed oxide, FeO·Fe$_2$O$_3$) is
questions.explanation: $3x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 3x = 8 \Rightarrow x = +8/3 \approx +2.67$, the average of one Fe$^{2+}$ and two Fe$^{3+}$ ions.
questions.trick: Mixed oxide = weighted average oxidation state; solve $3x+4(-2)=0$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A redox titration between oxalic acid and KMnO$_4$ in acidic medium requires heating because
options: oxalic acid is insoluble in cold water
the reaction is slow at room temperature and needs activation energy
the colour change is visible only when hot
questions.explanation: The oxidation of oxalate ions by MnO$_4^-$ has a high activation energy and proceeds slowly at room temperature, so the solution is usually warmed to about 60°C.
questions.trick: Slow room-temperature kinetics, not solubility, is why this titration needs heating.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following acts as an oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (Cr in +6) readily gets reduced to Cr$^{3+}$ (+3), making it a strong oxidising agent, commonly used in volumetric analysis.
questions.trick: An oxidising agent itself gets reduced — look for the species with a high, reducible oxidation state.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the reaction $2Na + Cl_2 \to 2NaCl$, sodium is
questions.explanation: Na (0) loses one electron to form Na$^+$ (+1): this is oxidation, by definition loss of electrons/increase in oxidation number.
questions.trick: Losing electrons (0 → positive ion) is oxidation, by definition.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A species with more negative standard reduction potential acts as a
questions.explanation: A very negative $E^\circ$ means the species has little tendency to be reduced (gain electrons) and instead readily loses electrons, i.e. it is a strong reducing agent.
questions.trick: More negative $E^\circ$ = weaker pull on electrons = stronger reducing agent.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The reaction $2KClO_3 \to 2KCl + 3O_2$ is an example of a
questions.explanation: One compound (KClO$_3$) breaks down into simpler substances (KCl and O$_2$), so this is a decomposition reaction. Within it, Cl goes from +5 to −1 (reduced) while O goes from −2 to 0 (oxidised) — an intramolecular redox change. It is not disproportionation, since that term applies when the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced; here Cl and O are different elements.
questions.trick: One compound → simpler substances = decomposition, even if redox occurs inside.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Fluorine shows an oxidation number of
questions.explanation: Being the most electronegative element, fluorine is always −1 in its compounds; it never shows a positive oxidation state.
questions.trick: Fluorine is the most electronegative element → always $-1$ in compounds, no exceptions.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The reaction $Cl_2 + 2OH^- \to Cl^- + ClO^- + H_2O$ is an example of
questions.explanation: Chlorine (0) is simultaneously reduced to Cl$^-$ (−1) and oxidised to ClO$^-$ (+1) — the same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction.
questions.trick: Same element split into two oxidation states → disproportionation.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the free radical Cl$_2$/CH$_4$ reaction, the propagation step Cl• + CH$_4$ → •CH$_3$ + HCl illustrates
options: a step where a bond is broken homolytically to generate a new radical
questions.explanation: Free-radical propagation proceeds by homolytic C-H bond cleavage: Cl• abstracts an H atom, generating HCl and a new methyl free radical, each fragment keeping one electron.
questions.trick: Radical propagation = homolytic bond cleavage generating a new radical.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which technique is used to separate a mixture of two miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 K?
questions.explanation: When boiling points are close, repeated vaporisation-condensation on a fractionating column (fractional distillation) is needed for good separation; simple distillation only works when the difference is large.
questions.trick: Close boiling points (<25 K apart) → fractional distillation, not simple.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Differential extraction is used to separate a compound from its aqueous solution by shaking it with an organic solvent because the compound is
options: more soluble in the organic solvent than in water, and can be repeatedly extracted with fresh portions
insoluble in both the aqueous and organic layers
questions.explanation: Differential (solvent) extraction relies on the compound being more soluble in an immiscible organic solvent than in water; repeated extraction with fresh solvent recovers it more completely than a single extraction.
questions.trick: Multiple small extractions beat one big one — think partition coefficient.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of C-C-C bond angles in sp$^3$, sp$^2$ and sp hybridised carbon centres is
questions.explanation: Bond angles are 109.5° (sp$^3$), 120° (sp$^2$) and 180° (sp), so the order is sp > sp$^2$ > sp$^3$.
questions.trick: More s-character → wider angle: sp(180°) > sp$^2$(120°) > sp$^3$(109.5°).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The cyclopropenyl cation (a 3-membered ring with 2 $\pi$ electrons) is aromatic according to Hückel's rule because it is
options: planar, cyclic, fully conjugated with $(4n+2)\pi$ electrons for n = 0 (2 $\pi$ electrons)
questions.explanation: It is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated with 2 $\pi$ electrons, satisfying $(4n+2)$ with n = 0, so despite being a non-benzenoid, 3-membered system it is aromatic.
questions.trick: Check planar + cyclic + conjugated + $(4n+2)\pi$ e⁻ for aromaticity.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct decreasing order of stability of the following carbocations: (I) $CH_3^+$ (II) $(CH_3)_3C^+$ (III) $(CH_3)_2CH^+$ is
questions.explanation: More alkyl groups give more hyperconjugation and +I effect, so 3° > 2° > 1° i.e. II > III > I.
questions.trick: Stability order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl carbocation, always.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A major limitation of Friedel-Crafts alkylation is that
options: the product ring becomes more activated towards further substitution, often leading to polyalkylation
it never forms a carbocation intermediate
it cannot use AlCl$_3$ as catalyst
it only works on aliphatic compounds
questions.explanation: Since alkyl groups are electron-donating (activating), the monoalkylated product is more reactive than benzene itself towards further electrophilic attack, commonly giving a mixture of polyalkylated products.
questions.trick: Alkyl group activates ring further → polyalkylation is FC alkylation's flaw.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Controlled hydrogenation of an alkyne using Lindlar's catalyst gives
questions.explanation: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/BaSO$_4$ poisoned with quinoline) adds H$_2$ syn to the triple bond, stopping at the cis (Z) alkene.
questions.trick: Lindlar's catalyst = syn addition, stops at cis alkene.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of acidic character of the C-H bond (ease of removing a proton) is
questions.explanation: Greater s-character of the C-H bond holds the bonding electrons closer to carbon, making the H more easily removed as H$^+$; s-character is sp (50%) > sp$^2$ (33%) > sp$^3$ (25%), so terminal alkyne > alkene > alkane in acidity.
questions.trick: More s-character holds electrons tighter → acidity: alkyne > alkene > alkane.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Nitration of toluene with conc. HNO$_3$/H$_2$SO$_4$ gives mainly
options: 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene directly in one step at room temperature
questions.explanation: -CH$_3$ is an activating, ortho/para-directing group (electron release by hyperconjugation/+I), so nitration gives predominantly o- and p-nitrotoluene.
questions.trick: -CH$_3$ is activating, o/p-directing → nitration gives o- and p-product.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Markovnikov's rule for addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene states that
options: H adds to the carbon bearing fewer hydrogens
H and X add randomly with equal probability
X (halogen) adds to the carbon bearing fewer hydrogens, via the more stable carbocation intermediate
the reaction proceeds only via a free-radical mechanism
questions.explanation: The proton adds first to give the more stable (more substituted) carbocation, so the halide ion then bonds to the carbon that originally had fewer H atoms.
questions.trick: Markovnikov: H adds to give the more stable carbocation, X follows.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of moles of O$_2$ required for the complete combustion of 2 moles of acetylene (C$_2$H$_2$) is
questions.explanation: $C_2H_2 + \dfrac{5}{2}O_2 \to 2CO_2 + H_2O$; for 1 mol C$_2$H$_2$, 2.5 mol O$_2$ is needed, so 2 mol C$_2$H$_2$ requires $2\times2.5 = 5$ mol O$_2$.
questions.trick: Write balanced combustion equation first, then scale O$_2$ by moles given.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Thermal or catalytic cracking of higher alkanes (as in petroleum refining) mainly produces
options: smaller alkanes and alkenes by breaking C-C bonds
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks C-C bonds in large alkane molecules (from petroleum) under heat/catalyst to give a mixture of smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes, e.g. for petrol and petrochemical feedstocks.
questions.trick: Cracking breaks C-C bonds → smaller alkanes + alkenes mixture.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene followed by treatment with Zn/H$_2$O gives
questions.explanation: 2-Methylbut-2-ene is (CH$_3$)$_2$C=CH-CH$_3$; ozonolysis cleaves the C=C giving (CH$_3$)$_2$C=O (acetone) and CH$_3$CHO (acetaldehyde).
questions.trick: Ozonolysis: split C=C, each carbon becomes C=O (replace =CH- with =O).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Complete catalytic hydrogenation of one mole of an alkyne (R-C$\equiv$C-R') to the corresponding alkane requires
questions.explanation: The triple bond first adds 1 mol H$_2$ to give an alkene, which adds a further 1 mol H$_2$ to give the alkane — 2 mol H$_2$ in total.
questions.trick: Alkyne → alkene → alkane: each step needs 1 mol H$_2$, so 2 total.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: 5.6 litres of an alkene at STP weighs 10.5 g. The alkene is
questions.explanation: Moles $= 5.6/22.4 = 0.25$. Molar mass $= 10.5/0.25 = 42$ g mol$^{-1}$. For C$_nH_{2n}$, $14n = 42 \Rightarrow n = 3$, i.e. propene (C$_3$H$_6$).
questions.trick: Find M from PV=nRT/STP, then match $14n$ (alkene) or $14n+2$ (alkane).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following statements about benzene's resonance energy is correct?
options: It is negative, showing benzene is less stable than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene
Its resonance energy ($\approx$152 kJ mol$^{-1}$) is the difference between the calculated (hypothetical Kekulé) and experimental heats of hydrogenation
It has zero resonance energy since it is fully conjugated
It equals the heat of hydrogenation of cyclohexene
questions.explanation: Resonance energy is the extra stability of the real delocalised benzene compared to the hypothetical Kekulé (cyclohexatriene) structure, measured as the difference between expected and observed heats of hydrogenation (about 152 kJ mol$^{-1}$).
questions.trick: Resonance energy = calculated (Kekulé) minus experimental heat of hydrogenation.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of possible structural (chain) isomers of hexane, C$_6$H$_{14}$, is
questions.explanation: Hexane has 5 structural isomers: n-hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,3-dimethylbutane and 2,2-dimethylbutane.
questions.trick: Memorize: hexane has exactly 5 chain isomers.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Dehydration of 2-methylbutan-2-ol with conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ gives predominantly (Zaitsev product)
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule favours the more substituted (more stable) alkene; removal of H from the more substituted adjacent carbon gives 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product.
questions.trick: Zaitsev: dehydration removes H from more-substituted carbon → more stable alkene.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The solubility of a solid in a liquid is largely unaffected by changes in pressure because
options: pressure only affects gaseous solutes, never solids
solubility is purely an electrical phenomenon
solids have very high vapour pressure
solids and liquids are only negligibly compressible
questions.explanation: Since solids and liquids do not compress appreciably under moderate pressure changes, pressure has essentially no effect on solid-in-liquid solubility (unlike gas solubility, which is pressure-dependent).
questions.trick: Solids/liquids barely compress → pressure doesn't affect their solubility.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: 2 g of a non-electrolyte dissolved in 50 g of water lowers the freezing point by 0.372 K. The molar mass of the solute is ($K_f = 1.86$ K kg mol$^{-1}$)
questions.trick: $M=\dfrac{K_f\times w_{solute}\times1000}{\Delta T_f\times w_{solvent}}$ — memorize this formula.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The osmotic pressure of a 0.1 M glucose solution at 300 K is ($R = 0.0821$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\pi = CRT = 0.1\times0.0821\times300 = 2.46$ atm.
questions.trick: $\pi=CRT$ — plug in C, R, T directly.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Pure water has a vapour pressure of 23.8 mmHg at 25 °C. Dissolving 1 mol of glucose in 9 mol of water gives a solution whose vapour pressure is approximately
questions.trick: $\Delta p=x_{solute}\times p^\circ$, then $p=p^\circ-\Delta p$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The solubility of most solid solutes in a liquid solvent generally increases with rising temperature when
questions.explanation: By Le Chatelier's principle, if dissolving the solute absorbs heat (endothermic), raising the temperature favours further dissolution, increasing solubility.
questions.trick: Endothermic dissolution → solubility rises with temperature (Le Chatelier).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Acetic acid dimerises in benzene. If the van't Hoff factor observed is 0.6, the degree of association is
questions.explanation: For association into a dimer ($n=2$): $i = 1+\left(\dfrac1n-1\right)\alpha = 1-0.5\alpha$. $0.6 = 1-0.5\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = 0.8 = 80\%$.
questions.trick: Association into dimer: $i=1-\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$; solve for $\alpha$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes an ideal solution?
options: Its formation is always accompanied by a large volume change
It obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations, with $\Delta H_{mix} = 0$ and $\Delta V_{mix} = 0$
It has strong A-B interactions compared to A-A and B-B
It always shows a maximum-boiling azeotrope
questions.explanation: An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the entire concentration range, and forms with no enthalpy or volume change ($\Delta H_{mix} = \Delta V_{mix} = 0$), because A-A, B-B and A-B interactions are essentially identical.
questions.trick: Ideal solution: obeys Raoult's law, $\Delta H_{mix}=\Delta V_{mix}=0$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: According to Henry's law, the solubility of a gas in a liquid at a given temperature is
options: proportional to the square of pressure
directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas
inversely proportional to the partial pressure
questions.explanation: $p = K_H x$: mole fraction of dissolved gas ∝ its partial pressure above the solution.
questions.trick: Henry's law: $p=K_Hx$, gas solubility $\propto$ partial pressure.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: 1.0 g of a protein of molar mass 100000 g mol$^{-1}$ is dissolved in enough water to make 100 mL of solution. Its osmotic pressure at 300 K is ($R = 0.0821$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: Moles $= 1.0/100000 = 10^{-5}$ mol; $C = 10^{-5}/0.1 = 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. $\pi = CRT = 10^{-4}\times0.0821\times300 \approx 2.46\times10^{-3}$ atm — very small, which is why osmotic pressure (not $\Delta T_f$ or $\Delta T_b$) is used for such dilute macromolecular solutions.
questions.trick: Tiny protein molarity → tiny $\pi=CRT$, that's why OP method suits proteins.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The van't Hoff factor for K$_2$SO$_4$ assuming complete dissociation is
questions.trick: Count ions from formula: K$_2$SO$_4$ → 2K$^+$+SO$_4^{2-}$ = 3, so i=3.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A 0.1 M KCl solution (assume complete dissociation, $i=2$) is isotonic with a glucose solution (non-electrolyte, $i=1$) of concentration
questions.explanation: Equal osmotic pressure requires $i_1C_1 = i_2C_2$: $2\times0.1 = 1\times C_2 \Rightarrow C_2 = 0.2$ M.
questions.trick: Isotonic condition: $i_1C_1=i_2C_2$ — solve for unknown C.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a colligative property?
questions.explanation: Viscosity depends on the specific nature/structure of the solute and solvent molecules, not merely on the number of solute particles, so it is not a colligative property.
questions.trick: Viscosity depends on solute identity, not particle count — not colligative.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Two ideal liquids A ($p_A^\circ = 200$ mmHg) and B ($p_B^\circ = 100$ mmHg) are mixed with $x_A = 0.4$ and $x_B = 0.6$. The total vapour pressure of the solution is
questions.explanation: $p_A = 0.4\times200 = 80$ mmHg; $p_B = 0.6\times100 = 60$ mmHg; $p_{total} = 80+60 = 140$ mmHg.
questions.trick: $p_{total}=x_Ap_A^\circ+x_Bp_B^\circ$ — just add weighted terms.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: If the experimentally determined (apparent) molar mass of a solute from a colligative property measurement is LOWER than its normal (formula) molar mass, the solute is
questions.explanation: Dissociation increases the number of particles, so the observed colligative effect is larger than expected; since apparent molar mass is inversely related to the colligative property, this shows up as a molar mass lower than the true (formula) value, i.e. $i>1$.
questions.trick: Lower apparent molar mass ⇒ more particles formed ⇒ dissociation, i>1.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: An azeotrope (constant boiling mixture) cannot be separated into its pure components by
questions.explanation: At the azeotropic composition the vapour and liquid have the same composition, so the mixture distils over unchanged; ordinary fractional distillation cannot separate it further.
questions.trick: Azeotrope: vapour = liquid composition → fractional distillation can't separate it.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A mixture showing negative deviation from Raoult's law is
questions.explanation: Chloroform forms hydrogen bonds with acetone, strengthening A–B interactions and lowering vapour pressure. Benzene–toluene is ideal.
questions.trick: H-bonding between unlike molecules → negative deviation (acetone+chloroform).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Relative lowering of vapour pressure of a dilute solution of a non-volatile solute is equal to
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{p^\circ - p}{p^\circ} = x_{solute}$ (Raoult's law).
questions.trick: $\dfrac{p^\circ-p}{p^\circ}=x_{solute}$ — relative lowering equals solute mole fraction.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Molality is preferred over molarity for precise work because
options: molality is based on mass of solvent, so it does not change with temperature, unlike molarity which is based on solution volume
molality is always numerically larger than molarity
questions.explanation: Since volume changes with temperature (thermal expansion) but mass does not, molality (mol per kg of solvent) remains constant with temperature while molarity (mol per litre of solution) does not.
questions.trick: Mass doesn't change with T, volume does → molality is T-independent.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A solution of a non-volatile solute always boils at a HIGHER temperature than the pure solvent because
options: the solute reacts with the solvent
the solute's vapour pressure lowers the solution's total vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed for it to equal atmospheric pressure
the solute increases the solution's vapour pressure
questions.explanation: Since the non-volatile solute lowers the solution's vapour pressure at any given temperature (Raoult's law), the solution must be heated to a higher temperature than the pure solvent before its vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure (boils).
questions.trick: Lower V.P. from solute → needs higher T to reach atmospheric pressure.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For an ideal solution of A and B in which the partial vapour pressure of A is $p_A = 80$ mmHg and the total vapour pressure is $p_{total} = 140$ mmHg, the mole fraction of A in the vapour phase is
questions.explanation: By Dalton's law, mole fraction of A in vapour $= p_A/p_{total} = 80/140 \approx 0.571$, which is richer in the more volatile component A than the liquid phase (0.4).
questions.trick: Vapour-phase mole fraction $=p_A/p_{total}$ (Dalton's law).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Solutions having the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature are called
questions.explanation: Isotonic — e.g. 0.9% (mass/volume) NaCl and blood plasma.
questions.trick: Same osmotic pressure at same T = isotonic solutions.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Ethanol–water (95.6% ethanol) forms
questions.explanation: Positive deviation from Raoult's law → minimum boiling azeotrope; pure ethanol cannot be obtained by fractional distillation.
questions.trick: Positive deviation + max V.P. → minimum-boiling azeotrope (ethanol-water).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The value of $K_H$ for N$_2$ is higher than that for O$_2$ in water at 298 K. This means
options: N$_2$ is more soluble than O$_2$
O$_2$ is more soluble than N$_2$
questions.explanation: $x = p/K_H$: a higher $K_H$ means lower solubility, so O$_2$ is more soluble than N$_2$.
questions.trick: $x=p/K_H$: higher $K_H$ means LOWER solubility.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The best colligative method for determining the molar mass of proteins and polymers is
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure is large even for dilute solutions, is measured at room temperature (no decomposition), and uses molarity.
questions.trick: Big proteins → osmotic pressure method (measurable at room T, dilute OK).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a 0.1 molal aqueous NaCl solution, the van't Hoff factor $i$ is found to be 1.87. The degree of dissociation of NaCl is
questions.explanation: $i = 1+(n-1)\alpha$ with $n=2$: $1.87 = 1+\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = 0.87 = 87\%$.
questions.trick: $i=1+(n-1)\alpha$; solve for $\alpha$ using n=2 for NaCl.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The SI-compatible unit commonly used to express the specific conductance (conductivity) of an electrolytic solution is
questions.explanation: Conductivity $\kappa$ is the reciprocal of resistivity and is expressed in siemens per centimetre (S cm$^{-1}$) or siemens per metre (S m$^{-1}$).
questions.trick: Conductivity's SI-friendly unit: S cm$^{-1}$ (or S m$^{-1}$).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary cell (non-rechargeable)?
questions.explanation: The Leclanché (dry) cell is a primary cell — once its reactants are consumed it cannot be recharged, unlike lead storage, Ni-Cd or Li-ion cells which are secondary (rechargeable).
questions.trick: Primary cell = one-use, cannot recharge (Leclanché/dry cell).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The same quantity of electricity is passed through separate cells of AgNO$_3$ and CuSO$_4$ solutions. If 5.4 g of Ag (M = 108) is deposited, the mass of Cu (M = 63.5) deposited is
questions.explanation: Moles of electrons $= 5.4/108 = 0.05$ mol e$^-$. Cu$^{2+}$ needs 2 e$^-$ per atom, so moles Cu $= 0.05/2 = 0.025$; mass $= 0.025\times63.5 = 1.588$ g.
questions.trick: Same charge → equal moles of e⁻; use $n_e=w/M$ then scale by valency.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The quantity of electricity required to deposit 1 mole of aluminium metal from molten Al$_2$O$_3$ (Al$^{3+}$ + 3e$^-$ $\to$ Al) is
questions.explanation: Since 3 electrons are needed per Al$^{3+}$ ion, 1 mole of Al requires 3 Faradays of charge $= 3\times96500 = 289500$ C.
questions.trick: Charge needed = n (electrons per ion) $\times$ 96500 C per mole.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In an electrolytic cell (unlike a galvanic cell), the anode is
questions.explanation: In electrolysis, the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the external battery and oxidation still occurs there — only the polarity convention differs from a galvanic cell (where the anode is negative).
questions.trick: Electrolytic cell: anode is still oxidation but wired to +ve terminal.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a redox couple with a very negative standard reduction potential (e.g. Li$^+$/Li, $E^\circ = -3.04$ V), the metal is
options: a very strong reducing agent, readily oxidised to its cation
a very poor reducing agent, difficult to oxidise
questions.explanation: A very negative reduction potential means the reverse (oxidation) reaction is highly favoured, so the metal readily loses electrons and acts as a strong reducing agent — Li is in fact the strongest reducing agent among common metals in aqueous solution.
questions.trick: Very negative $E^\circ_{red}$ → metal loses e⁻ easily → strong reducing agent.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a strong electrolyte, molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ varies with $\sqrt{C}$ according to the Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation as
questions.explanation: For strong electrolytes, $\Lambda_m$ decreases slightly with increasing concentration due to inter-ionic attractions, following $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{C}$; a plot of $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{C}$ is linear allowing extrapolation to get $\Lambda_m^\circ$.
questions.trick: Strong electrolyte: $\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^\circ-A\sqrt{C}$, linear in $\sqrt{C}$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Rusting of iron is best described as
options: a process that requires no moisture
an electrochemical process involving oxidation of Fe at anodic sites and reduction of O$_2$ at cathodic sites
a purely chemical reaction with no electron transfer
a physical adsorption of oxygen on iron
questions.explanation: Rusting is electrochemical corrosion: Fe is oxidised (Fe $\to$ Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$) at anodic spots, and O$_2$ is reduced at cathodic spots (with moisture as the medium), ultimately forming hydrated Fe$_2$O$_3$.
questions.trick: Rusting = electrochemical: Fe oxidised at anode spot, O$_2$ reduced at cathode spot.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Among common elements, fluorine (F$_2$/F$^-$) has the highest standard reduction potential, making it
options: the strongest oxidising agent among common species
questions.explanation: A high (very positive) standard reduction potential means the species is easily reduced, i.e. it is a strong oxidising agent; F$_2$ has the highest $E^\circ$ in the electrochemical series.
questions.trick: Most positive $E^\circ_{red}$ = easiest to reduce = strongest oxidiser (F$_2$).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In electroplating an object with a metal such as silver or chromium, the object to be plated is made the
questions.explanation: In electroplating (an electrolytic process), the object to be plated is connected as the cathode so that metal cations from the electrolyte are reduced and deposited onto its surface.
questions.trick: Electroplating: object to be plated = cathode (gets reduced metal).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For the cell reaction $Zn + Cu^{2+} \to Zn^{2+} + Cu$ with $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.10$ V, $\Delta G^\circ$ is (F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$, n = 2)
questions.explanation: $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell} = -2\times96500\times1.10 = -212300$ J mol$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ_{cell}$ — plug n, F, E directly.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In a lead storage battery during discharge, the electrode reactions convert PbO$_2$ and Pb into
questions.explanation: During discharge, Pb (anode) is oxidised to PbSO$_4$ and PbO$_2$ (cathode) is reduced to PbSO$_4$, consuming H$_2$SO$_4$ from the electrolyte.
questions.trick: Lead-acid discharge: both Pb and PbO$_2$ end up as PbSO$_4$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the chlor-alkali process (electrolysis of concentrated aqueous NaCl), the products formed are
options: Na metal at the cathode and Cl$_2$ at the anode
only NaOH, with no gaseous products
H$_2$ at the cathode, Cl$_2$ at the anode, and NaOH remains in solution
questions.explanation: Water is preferentially reduced at the cathode (giving H$_2$ and OH$^-$) rather than Na$^+$ (which has a much more negative reduction potential), while Cl$^-$ is oxidised at the anode to Cl$_2$; NaOH accumulates in the solution.
questions.trick: Chlor-alkali: water reduced (H$_2$) at cathode beats Na$^+$; Cl$^-$ oxidised at anode.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells are generally more efficient at converting chemical energy to useful work than conventional combustion (heat) engines because
options: fuel cells operate at very high temperatures
fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electrical energy, avoiding the intermediate heat-to-work conversion limited by Carnot efficiency
fuel cells do not use catalysts
questions.explanation: Combustion engines first convert chemical energy to heat, then heat to work, and are limited by Carnot (thermodynamic) efficiency; fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electrical energy, bypassing this limitation and achieving higher efficiency.
questions.trick: Fuel cells skip Carnot-limited heat→work step, going chemical→electrical directly.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For an electrolyte that furnishes $z$ charges per formula unit (e.g. $z=2$ for CuSO$_4$), the equivalent conductivity $\Lambda_{eq}$ is related to the molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ by
questions.explanation: Equivalent conductivity is molar conductivity divided by the number of charges (equivalents) furnished per formula unit, $\Lambda_{eq} = \Lambda_m/z$.
questions.trick: $\Lambda_{eq}=\Lambda_m/z$ — divide by charge number per formula unit.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The salt bridge in a galvanic cell mainly functions to
options: supply electrons to the external circuit
maintain electrical neutrality in each half-cell by allowing ion flow, completing the internal circuit
increase the EMF of the cell
act as the site of oxidation
questions.explanation: As the cell reaction proceeds, charge builds up in each half-cell; the salt bridge allows ions to migrate between the half-cells to maintain electrical neutrality and complete the circuit, while minimising the liquid-junction potential.
questions.trick: Salt bridge = ion flow to keep both half-cells electrically neutral.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A current of 2 A is passed for 965 seconds through molten NaCl. The mass of Na deposited is (Na = 23, F = 96500 C)
questions.explanation: Charge $= it = 2\times965 = 1930$ C $= 0.02$ F. Na$^+$ + e$^-$ $\to$ Na needs 1 F per mole, so mass $= 0.02\times23 = 0.46$ g.
questions.trick: $w=\dfrac{it}{F}\times M$ (n=1 for Na$^+$) — Faraday's first law.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a weak electrolyte, molar conductivity increases sharply with dilution mainly because
options: the degree of dissociation increases, producing more ions
questions.explanation: Weak electrolytes dissociate more as concentration decreases (dilution), producing more ions per mole and hence sharply higher molar conductivity, approaching $\Lambda_m^\circ$ only at infinite dilution.
questions.trick: Weak electrolyte: dilution boosts dissociation → $\Lambda_m$ shoots up.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: If $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.0591$ V and n = 1 for a cell at 298 K, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ of the reaction is
questions.explanation: $\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591} = \dfrac{1\times0.0591}{0.0591} = 1 \Rightarrow K_c = 10$.
questions.trick: $\log K_c=\dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591}$ — Nernst-derived shortcut.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a cell with n = 2 and $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.295$ V at 298 K, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ of the cell reaction is approximately
questions.explanation: $\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591} = \dfrac{2\times0.295}{0.0591} = \dfrac{0.59}{0.0591}\approx10$, so $K_c \approx 10^{10}$.
questions.trick: $\log K_c=\dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.0591}$; compute exponent then $K_c=10^{\text{exponent}}$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement about the Daniell cell, Zn(s)|Zn$^{2+}$(aq)||Cu$^{2+}$(aq)|Cu(s), is INCORRECT?
options: Electrons flow through the external circuit from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
The copper electrode acts as the anode, where oxidation occurs
The concentration of Cu$^{2+}$ ions decreases as the cell operates
The mass of the zinc electrode decreases as the cell operates
questions.explanation: In the Daniell cell, copper is the cathode (site of reduction, Cu$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$ $\to$ Cu); zinc is the anode (site of oxidation), so calling copper the anode is incorrect.
questions.trick: In Daniell cell Cu is always cathode (reduction), never anode.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For the cell reaction M(s) + N$^{2+}$(aq, 0.001 M) $\to$ M$^{2+}$(aq, 0.1 M) + N(s), with $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.30$ V, n = 2, the EMF at 298 K is (use $\dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log(100) = 0.0591$)
questions.trick: Nernst: $E_{cell}=E^\circ-\dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log Q$, Q = products/reactants conc.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Given $E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu} = 0.34$ V and $E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = -0.76$ V, the standard EMF of the Daniell cell is
questions.explanation: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10$ V (Cu is cathode, Zn is anode).
questions.trick: $E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}$ (right minus left).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The cell constant of a conductivity cell is defined as
options: the product of conductivity and molarity
the ratio of resistance to conductance
the ratio of the distance between the electrodes (l) to the area of cross-section (A)
questions.explanation: Cell constant $G^* = l/A$ is a fixed geometric property of the conductivity cell, used to convert measured conductance into conductivity: $\kappa = G^*\times G$ (G = measured conductance).
questions.trick: Cell constant $G^*=l/A$ — pure geometry of the conductivity cell.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For the concentration cell Cu(s)|Cu$^{2+}$(0.01 M)||Cu$^{2+}$(1 M)|Cu(s) at 298 K (n = 2), the EMF of the cell is
questions.explanation: For a concentration cell, $E^\circ_{cell}=0$, and $E_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{[Cu^{2+}]_{cathode}}{[Cu^{2+}]_{anode}} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{0.01} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\times2 = 0.0591$ V.
questions.trick: Concentration cell: $E_{cell}=\dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_{cathode}}{C_{anode}}$, $E^\circ=0$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The rate constant of a first-order reaction is 0.0693 min$^{-1}$. Its half-life is
questions.trick: $t_{1/2}=0.693/k$ for first order — direct plug-in.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction with $k = 0.05$ mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ and $[A]_0 = 0.5$ M, the half-life is
questions.trick: $t_{1/2}=[A]_0/2k$ for zero order — direct substitution.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $2\text{N}_2\text{O}_5 \to 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$, the rate of reaction in terms of NO$_2$ formation is
questions.explanation: Rate $= -\dfrac12\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = \dfrac14\dfrac{d[\text{NO}_2]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}$.
questions.trick: Divide by stoichiometric coefficient: rate $=\dfrac1{\text{coeff}}\dfrac{d[\text{product}]}{dt}$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The rate constant of a reaction has units of mol$^{-2}$ L$^2$ s$^{-1}$. The order of the reaction is
questions.explanation: Units of $k$ are $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}$ s$^{-1}$. Here $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n} = \text{mol}^{-2}\text{L}^2 = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{-2}$, so $1-n=-2 \Rightarrow n=3$.
questions.trick: Match k's units to $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}$ and solve for n.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, a plot of $[A]$ (concentration of reactant) versus time $t$ is
options: a straight line with slope $-k$ and intercept $[A]_0$
a straight line through the origin with slope $+k$
a curve that is independent of $[A]_0$
questions.explanation: $[A] = [A]_0 - kt$ is linear in $t$, with intercept $[A]_0$ and a negative slope of magnitude $k$.
questions.trick: Zero order: $[A]=[A]_0-kt$, straight line, slope $-k$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, plotting which quantity against time $t$ gives a straight line?
questions.explanation: $\ln[A] = \ln[A]_0 - kt$ is linear in $t$ with slope $-k$; this graphical test distinguishes a first-order reaction from zero or second order.
questions.trick: First order gives straight line only for $\ln[A]$ (or $\log[A]$) vs t.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester (saponification), $CH_3COOC_2H_5 + OH^- \to CH_3COO^- + C_2H_5OH$, is typically
questions.explanation: Unlike acid hydrolysis (where water is in large excess), saponification with OH$^-$ depends on the concentrations of both the ester and hydroxide ion, making it a genuine second-order, bimolecular reaction.
questions.trick: Saponification (OH$^-$ + ester) depends on both → true second order.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 min. The time taken for the concentration to fall from 0.8 M to 0.2 M is
questions.explanation: 0.8 → 0.4 → 0.2 is two half-lives = 40 min.
questions.trick: Count halvings: 0.8→0.4→0.2 is 2 half-lives, multiply by $t_{1/2}$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A first-order reaction has $k = 1\times10^{-6}$ s$^{-1}$ at 300 K and activation energy $E_a = 22.97$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Using $2.303RT \approx 5742$ J mol$^{-1}$ at 300 K, the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor $A$ is approximately
questions.trick: $\log A=\log k+\dfrac{E_a}{2.303RT}$ — rearranged Arrhenius equation.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a reaction that is zero order with respect to reactant X, doubling the initial concentration of X
options: has no effect on the rate
questions.explanation: Since rate $= k[X]^0 = k$, the rate is independent of $[X]$, so changing its concentration (while it remains present) does not change the rate.
questions.trick: Zero order in X → rate = k, unaffected by changing [X].
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the time required for 75% completion is
questions.explanation: 100% → 50% → 25% remaining takes two half-lives.
questions.trick: 75% done = 25% left = $(1/2)^2$ → exactly 2 half-lives.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The order of a chemical reaction can be determined
options: only experimentally, from the observed dependence of rate on concentration
directly from the balanced stoichiometric equation
questions.explanation: Unlike molecularity, the order of a reaction is an experimental quantity found from rate data; it cannot be predicted merely from the balanced equation since most reactions proceed through multiple elementary steps.
questions.trick: Order is ALWAYS found by experiment, never assumed from stoichiometry.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is left unaffected by the addition of a catalyst to a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
options: The time taken to reach equilibrium
The activation energy of the forward reaction
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers $E_a$ for both forward and reverse reactions equally, speeding up how quickly equilibrium is reached, but it does not change $\Delta G^\circ$, so the equilibrium constant $K$ remains unchanged.
questions.trick: Catalyst speeds both directions equally → K unchanged, only rate changes.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A radioactive isotope (which decays by first-order kinetics) loses 75% of its activity in 30 minutes. Its half-life is
questions.explanation: 75% decayed means 25% $= (1/2)^2$ remains, i.e. 2 half-lives have elapsed in 30 min, so $t_{1/2} = 30/2 = 15$ min.
questions.trick: 25% remaining $=(1/2)^2$ → 2 half-lives elapsed; divide time by 2.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the Arrhenius equation $k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, the factor $e^{-E_a/RT}$ represents
options: the rate constant at infinite temperature
the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ $E_a$
questions.explanation: It is the Boltzmann fraction of molecules having kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. $A$ is the frequency (pre-exponential) factor.
questions.trick: $e^{-E_a/RT}$ = Boltzmann fraction with energy ≥ $E_a$; A is frequency factor.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a reaction with rate $= k[A]^2[B]$, if the concentrations of both A and B are doubled, the rate becomes
questions.explanation: $2^2\times2 = 8$ times.
questions.trick: Multiply exponents: doubling both A(²) and B(¹) → $2^2\times2^1=8$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In collision theory, the steric (probability) factor $P$ accounts for the fact that
options: all collisions between reactant molecules lead to products
not all collisions with sufficient energy result in a reaction, since molecules must also be oriented favourably
temperature has no effect on reaction rate
questions.explanation: Even when colliding molecules have energy $\ge E_a$, they must also collide with the correct relative orientation for bonds to form/break; $P$ (usually $<1$) corrects the simple collision frequency for this requirement.
questions.trick: Steric factor P corrects for molecular orientation, not just energy.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The decomposition of N$_2$O$_5$, $2N_2O_5 \to 4NO_2+O_2$, is experimentally found to be first order overall, even though the stoichiometric coefficient of N$_2$O$_5$ is 2. This illustrates that
options: order is an experimental quantity that need not match the stoichiometric coefficients, since the reaction proceeds via a multi-step mechanism
order is the same as molecularity for this reaction
order must always equal the sum of stoichiometric coefficients
questions.explanation: Order is determined only by experiment and reflects the rate-determining step of the actual (often multi-step) mechanism, so it need not equal the coefficients of the overall balanced equation.
questions.trick: Order need NOT match stoichiometric coefficients — it's experimental (multi-step mechanism).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of an ester, water (a reactant in the balanced equation) has an order of essentially zero with respect to rate. This is because
options: water does not participate in the mechanism at all
order must always be zero for any solvent
water is present in such large excess that its concentration remains effectively constant during the reaction
questions.explanation: Since water is the solvent and present in huge excess, its concentration barely changes during the reaction, so the rate appears independent of $[H_2O]$ even though it is a reactant — this is the basis of pseudo-order kinetics.
questions.trick: Large-excess reactant (solvent water) has effectively constant, so 'zero' order.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following graphs is a straight line specifically for a FIRST-order reaction (and not for a zero-order reaction)?
questions.explanation: $[A]$ vs $t$ is linear only for a zero-order reaction; for a first-order reaction it is $\log[A]$ (or $\ln[A]$) vs $t$ that gives a straight line, with slope $-k/2.303$.
questions.trick: Zero order: [A] vs t linear; first order: log[A] vs t linear.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: As temperature increases, the rate constant $k$ of a reaction generally increases mainly because
options: a larger fraction of molecules acquire kinetic energy $\ge E_a$, per the Boltzmann distribution
questions.explanation: According to the Boltzmann distribution, the fraction of molecules with energy $\ge E_a$ (given by $e^{-E_a/RT}$) increases sharply with temperature, increasing the rate constant $k$, even though $E_a$ itself is unchanged.
questions.trick: Rate rises with T because $e^{-E_a/RT}$ (fraction with E≥$E_a$) grows, not $E_a$ itself.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The half-life of a zero-order reaction is
options: proportional to the square of initial concentration
questions.explanation: $t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k$ for zero order.
questions.trick: Zero order: $t_{1/2}=[A]_0/2k$ — proportional to initial conc.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $A+B\to$ products, doubling $[A]$ (keeping $[B]$ constant) doubles the rate, while doubling $[B]$ (keeping $[A]$ constant) has no effect on the rate. The order of the reaction with respect to A and the overall order are respectively
questions.explanation: Rate $\propto [A]^1$ since doubling A doubles rate; rate is independent of B ($[B]^0$), so overall order $= 1+0 = 1$.
questions.trick: Rate unaffected by a reactant → its order is 0; sum orders for overall.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the time required for 87.5% completion, in terms of the half-life $t_{1/2}$, is
questions.explanation: 87.5% completion leaves 12.5% $= (1/2)^3$ of the reactant, which takes exactly 3 successive half-lives: $t = 3t_{1/2}$.
questions.trick: 12.5% left $=(1/2)^3$ → exactly 3 half-lives for 87.5% completion.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $P+Q\to$ products: doubling $[P]$ (constant $[Q]$) doubles the rate; doubling $[Q]$ (constant $[P]$) makes the rate four times. The overall order of the reaction is
questions.explanation: Rate $\propto [P]^1[Q]^2$ (doubling P doubles rate → order 1 in P; doubling Q gives $2^2=4\times$ rate → order 2 in Q). Overall order $= 1+2 = 3$.
questions.trick: Match rate-multiplier to power of 2: 2× rate→order 1, 4×→order 2.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In acidic medium, the equivalent weight of KMnO$_4$ (molar mass M) used as an oxidising agent (Mn$^{7+}\to$Mn$^{2+}$) is
questions.explanation: In acidic medium MnO$_4^-$ accepts 5 electrons per formula unit (Mn$^{7+}\to$Mn$^{2+}$), so its equivalent weight is molar mass divided by 5.
questions.trick: Eq. wt of KMnO$_4$ = M/(electrons gained): acidic medium → M/5.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which ion is colourless due to a $d^0$ configuration?
questions.explanation: Sc$^{3+}$ has configuration [Ar]3d$^0$ — with no d electrons, d-d transitions are impossible, so the ion is colourless. Ti$^{3+}$(d$^1$), V$^{3+}$(d$^2$) and Cr$^{3+}$(d$^3$) are all coloured.
questions.trick: $d^0$ or $d^{10}$ configuration → no d-d transition → colourless.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Interstitial compounds formed by transition metals with small atoms like C, N, H are typically
options: hard, high melting, and chemically inert, retaining metallic conductivity
questions.explanation: Small non-metal atoms occupy interstitial voids in the metal lattice without disrupting the metallic bonding much, giving compounds (e.g. steel, TiC) that are hard, have high melting points and retain metallic conductivity.
questions.trick: Small atoms in interstitial voids → hard, high-melting, still metallic (steel).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Compared to lanthanoids, actinoids show
options: a wider range of oxidation states because 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy
a narrower range of oxidation states
questions.explanation: In actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s energy levels are comparable, allowing more electrons to participate in bonding, so actinoids show a greater variety of oxidation states than lanthanoids.
questions.trick: Actinoids: 5f/6d/7s close in energy → wider oxidation-state range than lanthanoids.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement about the maximum oxidation states of d-block elements is CORRECT?
options: The maximum oxidation state generally corresponds to the total number of $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons, rising to a peak around the middle of the series (e.g. Mn shows +7, matching its group number)
The maximum oxidation state decreases smoothly and continuously from Sc to Zn
d-block elements never show oxidation states higher than +3
The maximum oxidation state is always +2, regardless of the element
questions.explanation: Early-to-middle transition metals can use both their $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons in bonding, so the maximum oxidation state tends to rise towards the group number (e.g. Mn, group 7, reaches +7 in KMnO$_4$), before falling again towards the later members like Cu and Zn.
questions.trick: Max oxidation state ≈ total (n-1)d+ns electrons, peaks near group number (Mn=+7).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A major consequence of lanthanoid contraction is that
options: 4d and 5d transition elements of the same group have almost identical atomic radii and similar properties
actinoids become more reactive than lanthanoids
questions.explanation: Because of lanthanoid contraction, the atomic radii of second (4d) and third (5d) row transition elements in the same group become nearly equal (e.g. Zr and Hf), making their chemical properties very similar and hard to separate.
questions.trick: Lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d congeners nearly same size (Zr≈Hf).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The maximum oxidation state shown by any d-block element (+8) is exhibited by
questions.explanation: Ruthenium and osmium (group 8) can attain the +8 oxidation state, e.g. in OsO$_4$, the highest oxidation state known among the d-block elements.
questions.trick: +8 is the ceiling of d-block oxidation states: only Ru and Os reach it.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In neutral or faintly alkaline medium, KMnO$_4$ oxidises reactants and itself is reduced to
questions.explanation: In neutral/faintly alkaline medium, $MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- \to MnO_2 + 4OH^-$, a 3-electron reduction from Mn(+7) to Mn(+4), giving a brown MnO$_2$ precipitate.
questions.trick: Neutral/alkaline KMnO$_4$: Mn$^{7+}$→Mn$^{4+}$ (MnO$_2$, brown ppt, 3 e⁻).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Transition metals readily form a large number of complex compounds mainly because they have
options: no ability to form coordinate bonds
large atomic size, low charge and no vacant orbitals
completely filled d-orbitals in all oxidation states
small ionic size, relatively high ionic charge, and vacant low-energy d-orbitals available to accept ligand lone pairs
questions.explanation: Their small size, high charge density and empty/partially filled d-orbitals allow transition metal ions to strongly accept electron pairs donated by ligands, favouring extensive complex (coordination compound) formation.
questions.trick: Small size + high charge + empty d-orbitals = strong ligand-accepting ability.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In acidic medium, the equivalent weight of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (molar mass M) as an oxidising agent (2Cr$^{6+}\to$2Cr$^{3+}$) is
questions.explanation: One mole of Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ accepts 6 electrons overall (2 Cr atoms each gaining 3 electrons), so its equivalent weight is molar mass divided by 6.
questions.trick: Eq. wt of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ = M/6 (2 Cr atoms × 3 e⁻ each).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which lanthanoid commonly and stably shows a +4 oxidation state in addition to the usual +3, because the resulting ion attains a noble (f$^0$) configuration?
questions.explanation: Ce$^{4+}$ has an empty 4f subshell ($4f^0$), which is an extra-stable configuration, so cerium readily and stably shows +4 in addition to its usual +3 state (e.g. ceric ammonium sulphate, CAS, as an oxidant).
questions.trick: Ce$^{4+}$ reaches stable empty $4f^0$ → Ce is the +4-showing lanthanoid.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The spin-only magnetic moment of $Mn^{2+}$ (d$^5$, high spin, 5 unpaired electrons) is
questions.explanation: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM with n = 5: $\mu = \sqrt{5\times7} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92$ BM.
questions.trick: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM, n = unpaired electrons.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following 3d ions has exactly 3 unpaired electrons?
questions.explanation: Cr$^{3+}$ has configuration $t_{2g}^3$ ($d^3$), with one electron in each of the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals, giving 3 unpaired electrons; Mn$^{2+}$(d$^5$) has 5, and Zn$^{2+}$/Ti$^{4+}$ have none.
questions.trick: Count unpaired in $t_{2g}$/$e_g$: Cr$^{3+}$ (d$^3$) = 3 unpaired electrons.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Across the first transition series (Sc to Zn), the general trend in atomic radii is
options: a decrease initially, becoming roughly constant in the middle, then a slight increase near Cu, Zn
questions.explanation: Radii decrease initially due to increasing nuclear charge, level off around the middle (Cr-Fe) as d-electron shielding roughly balances increasing charge, and rise slightly near Cu and Zn due to increased electron-electron repulsion in the filled d subshell.
questions.trick: Radii trend across series: dip, flatten mid-series, tick up near Cu/Zn.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The contraction in atomic/ionic radii across the actinoid series (actinoid contraction) is GREATER, element for element, than the lanthanoid contraction mainly because
options: 5f orbitals shield more effectively than 4f orbitals
5f orbitals are more diffuse and shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than 4f orbitals do
questions.explanation: The 5f orbitals are more diffuse than 4f orbitals and shield the increasing nuclear charge even less effectively, so the actinoid contraction per element is somewhat larger than the corresponding lanthanoid contraction.
questions.trick: 5f more diffuse than 4f, shields worse → actinoid contraction > lanthanoid contraction.
questions.subject: chemistry
