questions.q: Transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts mainly because of their
options: ability to show variable oxidation states and form unstable intermediates with reactants
questions.explanation: Variable oxidation states let transition metals form intermediate complexes with reactants and provide alternative reaction pathways with lower activation energy, and their surfaces can adsorb reactant molecules (e.g. Fe in the Haber process, V$_2$O$_5$ in the Contact process).
questions.trick: Variable oxidation states + intermediate complex formation = good catalysis.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Number of unpaired electrons in Fe$^{3+}$ (3d$^5$, high spin) and its corresponding magnetic moment are
questions.explanation: Fe$^{3+}$ is $3d^5$; in the high-spin free ion all 5 electrons are unpaired (one per orbital), giving $\mu = \sqrt{5\times7} = 5.92$ BM.
questions.trick: Fe$^{3+}$ is d$^5$ high-spin → 5 unpaired e⁻ → $\mu=5.92$ BM (same as Mn$^{2+}$).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Misch metal, used in lighter flints, is an alloy consisting mainly of
options: a lanthanoid metal (mostly cerium, about 95%) along with iron and traces of S, C, Ca, Al
questions.explanation: Misch metal is approximately 95% lanthanoid metal (mainly cerium) with about 5% iron and traces of other elements; it sparks readily on friction, making it useful in cigarette lighter flints.
questions.trick: Misch metal = ~95% lanthanoid (mostly Ce) + Fe + traces — used in flints.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Zn, Cd and Hg are not regarded as typical transition elements because
options: they have completely filled $(n-1)d^{10}$ configuration in the ground state as well as common oxidation states, so they cannot show d-d transitions
questions.explanation: Zn, Cd, Hg have $d^{10}$ configuration in both the elemental and common (+2) oxidation states, so they lack partially filled d orbitals and hence do not show typical transition metal properties like colour and variable oxidation states.
questions.trick: Zn/Cd/Hg have full $d^{10}$ always → not true transition metals.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: $[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4$ and $[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br$ are examples of
questions.explanation: These two compounds give different ions in solution (Br$^-$ vs SO$_4^{2-}$ as the free counter ion) despite having the same molecular formula, characteristic of ionisation isomerism.
questions.trick: Different free ion released in water $\to$ ionisation isomerism.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In an octahedral complex, the crystal field splitting energy $\Delta_o$ depends on which factors?
options: colour of the counter ion only
the nature of the ligand, the charge on the metal ion, and whether the metal is 3d, 4d or 5d
molecular formula of the complex only
atomic mass of the metal only
questions.explanation: $\Delta_o$ increases with ligand field strength (spectrochemical series), with increasing metal oxidation state (more charge draws ligands closer), and going down a group (4d, 5d metals split more than 3d).
questions.trick: $\Delta_o$ rises with ligand strength, higher metal charge, and going 3d$\to$4d$\to$5d.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The oxidation state of iron in $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ is
questions.explanation: CN$^-$ ligands each carry a $-1$ charge; 6 CN$^-$ give $-6$. For overall charge $-4$: $x + (-6) = -4 \Rightarrow x = +2$.
questions.trick: Balance charge: metal + (ligand charges) = overall ionic charge.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The coordination number and oxidation number of platinum in $[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]$ are
questions.explanation: Each en is bidentate (2 donor atoms each, so 2 en = 4) plus 2 Cl = coordination number 6. en is neutral, Cl$^-$ contributes $-2$, so for the neutral complex Pt is $+2$ (Pt $+ 0 + (-2) = 0$).
questions.trick: Bidentate en gives 2 donor atoms each; count donors, then balance charge for oxidation state.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Linkage isomerism is possible in $[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2$ because the nitrito ligand can bind through
options: carbon in one form and nitrogen in the other
either its nitrogen atom (nitro, -NO$_2$) or an oxygen atom (nitrito, -ONO)
questions.explanation: NO$_2^-$ is an ambidentate ligand: it can coordinate via N (nitro form) or via O (nitrito form), giving rise to linkage isomers of the same overall formula.
questions.trick: NO$_2^-$ ambidentate: nitro binds via N, nitrito binds via O.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of geometrical isomers possible for the square planar complex $[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]$ is
questions.explanation: A square planar MA$_2$B$_2$ complex can have the two identical ligands adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) to each other, giving exactly 2 geometrical isomers.
questions.trick: Square planar MA$_2$B$_2$ always gives exactly cis + trans = 2 isomers.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: According to IUPAC rules, when naming a complex ion with more than one kind of ligand, the ligands are cited in the name in
options: alphabetical order, irrespective of their number or charge
questions.explanation: IUPAC nomenclature lists ligand names alphabetically (ignoring multiplying prefixes like di-, tri-, bis-), before naming the central metal atom.
questions.trick: Ligands cited alphabetically in the name; ignore di-/tri-/bis- prefixes for ordering.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The IUPAC name of $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$ is
questions.explanation: The complex anion is named first with ligands alphabetically, then the metal with suffix '-ate' since the ion is anionic, and its oxidation state: Fe is $+2$ since 6 CN$^-$ give $-6$ and overall charge is $-4$, so K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] = potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II).
questions.trick: Balance charge for oxidation state; anionic complex $\to$ metal name ends '-ate'.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The IUPAC name of $[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3$ is
questions.explanation: The cation is named first (ligands alphabetically then metal with oxidation state in Roman numerals), followed by the anion name: hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.
questions.trick: Name order: cation first, ligands alphabetical, then metal(oxidation state), anion last.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In naming coordination compounds, if the complex ion is a cation and the central metal is iron, the name used is
questions.explanation: When the coordination entity is a cation (or neutral), the metal's usual English name is used (e.g. iron, cobalt); the Latin-derived '-ate' form (ferrate) is used only when the complex ion is an anion.
questions.trick: Cation/neutral complex keeps normal metal name; only anionic complex uses '-ate'.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a double salt from a coordination compound?
options: A coordination compound loses its identity in solution, while a double salt retains the identity of its constituent ions
Double salts do not exist in crystalline form
A double salt completely dissociates into simple ions in solution, while a coordination compound retains its complex ion largely intact
questions.explanation: Double salts like Mohr's salt, FeSO$_4$.(NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$.6H$_2$O, dissociate completely into their simple constituent ions in solution and lose identity, whereas complex ions like $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ remain intact and do not give free Fe$^{2+}$ or CN$^-$ tests.
questions.trick: Double salt fully dissociates (loses identity); complex ion stays intact in solution.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: According to crystal field theory, in an octahedral complex the d orbitals split into
options: all five orbitals of equal energy
questions.explanation: In an octahedral field, ligands approach along the axes, raising the energy of $d_{z^2}, d_{x^2-y^2}$ ($e_g$) more than $d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{zx}$ ($t_{2g}$), which lie between the axes; so $t_{2g}$ is lower and $e_g$ is higher, separated by $\Delta_o$.
questions.trick: Octahedral: ligands hit $e_g$ head-on (higher), miss $t_{2g}$ (lower).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In Werner's theory, the secondary valency of a metal ion corresponds to its
questions.explanation: Werner defined secondary valency as the fixed number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal in a definite spatial arrangement — this is what we now call the coordination number.
questions.trick: Werner: secondary valency = fixed ligand count = coordination number.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is used in the extraction of silver and gold via complex formation?
questions.explanation: Silver and gold ores are leached with dilute NaCN solution in the presence of air; the metals form soluble cyanide complexes $[Ag(CN)_2]^-$/$[Au(CN)_2]^-$, from which the pure metal is later displaced by a more reactive metal like zinc.
questions.trick: Ag/Au leaching: dilute NaCN forms soluble $[M(CN)_2]^-$ complexes.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The number of unpaired electrons in the low-spin octahedral complex $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ (Fe$^{2+}$, $d^6$) is
questions.explanation: CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand; all six $d^6$ electrons pair up in the lower $t_{2g}$ orbitals ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), leaving zero unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).
questions.trick: Strong field CN$^-$ forces all $d^6$ electrons into $t_{2g}$ $\to$ zero unpaired.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following pairs correctly matches the ligand with its denticity?
questions.explanation: NH$_3$ has a single donor atom (N) and is unidentate; en is bidentate (two N donors), oxalate is bidentate (two O donors), and Cl$^-$ is unidentate.
questions.trick: Denticity: NH$_3$/Cl$^-$ unidentate; en/oxalate bidentate (two donor atoms).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Cisplatin, $[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]$ (cis isomer), is used clinically as
questions.explanation: cis-[Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$] (cisplatin) binds to DNA in cancer cells and inhibits replication, and is widely used as an anticancer chemotherapy drug; the trans isomer is biologically inactive.
questions.trick: cis-Platin fights cancer; trans isomer is biologically inactive.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following ligands, upon coordination, is classified as a $\pi$-acid (strong field) ligand due to back bonding?
questions.explanation: CO accepts electron density from filled metal d orbitals into its empty $\pi^*$ orbitals (synergic back bonding), which strengthens the metal-ligand bond and makes CO one of the strongest field ligands.
questions.trick: $\pi$-acid ligands (CO) back-bond into empty $\pi^*$ orbitals, becoming strong field.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following ligands is an example of an ambidentate ligand?
questions.explanation: An ambidentate ligand can coordinate through either of two different donor atoms; thiocyanate can bind through S (-SCN) or N (-NCS), unlike en (bidentate, N,N-donor) or oxalate (bidentate, O,O-donor).
questions.trick: Ambidentate = two possible donor atoms; SCN$^-$ binds via S or N.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which reaction of an alkyl halide proceeds with inversion of configuration?
questions.explanation: S$_N$2 is a single-step backside attack by the nucleophile, giving Walden inversion at the stereocentre.
questions.trick: Backside attack = inversion; that's S$_N$2, always.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the reactivity of haloarenes towards electrophilic substitution is correct?
options: Halogen substituents are ortho, para-directing but deactivating (net electron withdrawal by induction exceeds donation by resonance)
Halogen substituents are meta-directing and activating
Halogens have no directing effect on the ring
Halogen substituents are ortho, para-directing and strongly activating
questions.explanation: Halogens donate electron density into the ring by resonance (directing electrophiles to o,p) but withdraw more strongly by induction overall, making the ring less reactive than benzene itself even while directing o,p.
questions.trick: Halogens: o,p-directing by resonance but net deactivating by stronger induction.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct reactivity order of alkyl halides towards a given nucleophile under S$_N$2 conditions?
options: all react at identical rates regardless of the halogen
questions.explanation: Iodide is the best leaving group among halides (weakest C–X bond, most stable leaving anion), so alkyl iodides react fastest in S$_N$2 reactions: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
questions.trick: Best leaving group wins S$_N$2 rate: RI $>$ RBr $>$ RCl $>$ RF.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Vinyl halides and aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution mainly because
options: the halogen is attached to an sp$^2$ carbon and the C–X bond has partial double-bond character from resonance
they contain no C–X bond at all
they have no halogen lone pairs
questions.explanation: In both vinyl and aryl halides, the halogen lone pair conjugates with the adjacent $\pi$ system, shortening and strengthening the C–X bond and making it resistant to nucleophilic displacement.
questions.trick: sp$^2$ C-X with resonance double-bond character resists nucleophilic attack (vinyl/aryl).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Chlorobenzene is less reactive than alkyl chlorides towards nucleophilic substitution mainly because
options: chlorine is a poor leaving group in chlorobenzene
chlorine is more electronegative in the ring
resonance gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character
questions.explanation: Delocalisation of a lone pair of Cl into the ring shortens and strengthens the C–Cl bond and makes the carbon less electrophilic, hindering nucleophilic attack.
questions.trick: Aryl halides: resonance gives C-X partial double bond, kills substitution.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Freons are chemically
questions.explanation: Freons (e.g. CCl$_2$F$_2$, Freon-12) are chlorofluorocarbons used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants; they deplete stratospheric ozone.
questions.trick: Freons = CFCs of methane/ethane; refrigerants that deplete ozone.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The Wurtz reaction converts an alkyl halide into
questions.explanation: 2 RX + 2Na $\xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}}$ R–R + 2NaX, giving a symmetrical alkane with double the carbon chain.
questions.trick: Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na $\to$ symmetrical alkane, doubling carbon chain.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which alkyl halide would react fastest with KI in acetone (Finkelstein reaction)?
questions.explanation: The Finkelstein reaction proceeds by S$_N$2; less steric hindrance around the carbon favours faster reaction, so unhindered primary 1-chlorobutane reacts fastest among these, while the very hindered neopentyl halide reacts extremely slowly despite being primary.
questions.trick: Finkelstein is S$_N$2: least hindered primary halide reacts fastest with KI.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Chlorobenzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of FeCl$_3$ to give mainly
questions.explanation: Cl is an ortho, para director in electrophilic aromatic substitution due to resonance donation of a lone pair; para is major due to less steric hindrance.
questions.trick: Halogens are o,p-directors (resonance donation); para favoured, less steric clash.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which reaction is used to convert chlorobenzene into phenol industrially (Dow process)?
options: Fusion with NaOH at 623 K, 300 atm, followed by acidification
Treatment with dilute HCl at room temperature
questions.explanation: Chlorobenzene is hydrolysed to phenol only under forcing conditions (623 K, 300 atm NaOH) because the C–Cl bond is strengthened by resonance; this harsh requirement is the Dow process.
questions.trick: Dow process: chlorobenzene $\to$ phenol needs harsh 623 K, 300 atm NaOH.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Chloroform is stored in dark-coloured bottles, completely filled, with a little ethanol added, mainly to prevent
options: its oxidation by air and light to the poisonous gas phosgene
questions.explanation: Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of light to phosgene (COCl$_2$), a poisonous gas; ethanol converts any phosgene formed into harmless diethyl carbonate.
questions.trick: Chloroform + air/light $\to$ toxic phosgene; ethanol traps it, dark bottle prevents it.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: An alkyl halide is treated with sodium metal in the presence of dry ether to give an alkane of double the carbon count. If ethyl bromide is used, the product formed is
questions.explanation: 2 CH$_3$CH$_2$Br + 2Na $\to$ CH$_3$CH$_2$–CH$_2$CH$_3$ (n-butane) + 2NaBr, the Wurtz reaction, doubling the carbon chain of the starting alkyl halide.
questions.trick: Wurtz doubles carbon count: ethyl bromide $\to$ n-butane.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The relative rate of S$_N$2 reaction for methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary halides is
options: all react at the same rate
questions.explanation: S$_N$2 requires backside attack; increasing alkyl substitution increases steric hindrance, so methyl halides react fastest and tertiary halides essentially do not undergo S$_N$2.
questions.trick: S$_N$2 rate falls with bulk: methyl $>$ 1$^\circ$ $>$ 2$^\circ$ $>$ 3$^\circ$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A compound C$_4$H$_9$Br reacts with alcoholic KOH to give only one alkene as the elimination product (no isomeric alkenes possible). The compound is most likely
questions.explanation: tert-Butyl bromide, (CH$_3$)$_3$CBr, has only one type of $\beta$-hydrogen (from the three equivalent methyl groups), so elimination gives a single alkene, 2-methylpropene, with no other regiochemical possibility.
questions.trick: Only one type of $\beta$-H (symmetric methyls) $\to$ single elimination alkene possible.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following would undergo the fastest hydrolysis by an S$_N$1 mechanism in aqueous acetone?
questions.explanation: Benzyl chloride ionises readily because the resulting benzylic carbocation is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into the aromatic ring, favouring S$_N$1; aryl and vinyl halides do not ionise due to the strong, resonance-shortened C–Cl bond.
questions.trick: Benzylic C-X ionises fast: resonance-stabilised carbocation favours S$_N$1.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the preparation of Grignard reagents from aryl halides is correct?
options: Only alkyl halides with more than 10 carbons form Grignard reagents
Aryl halides such as bromobenzene can react with Mg in dry ether to form aryl magnesium halides, e.g. C$_6$H$_5$MgBr
Aryl halides can only form Grignard reagents in aqueous medium
Aryl halides never react with Mg under any conditions
questions.explanation: Unlike nucleophilic substitution (which fails on aryl halides), Grignard reagent formation is an oxidative insertion of Mg into the C–X bond and works for aryl halides too, giving aryl magnesium halides like phenylmagnesium bromide.
questions.trick: Grignard formation is Mg insertion into C-X; works on aryl halides too.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: 3.0 g of a monochloroalkane (C$_n$H$_{2n+1}$Cl) contains 0.71 g of chlorine (Cl, atomic mass 35.5). The approximate mass percentage of chlorine in the compound is used to identify n. What is the mass percentage of Cl?
questions.explanation: Mass % Cl = (0.71/3.0) $\times$ 100 $\approx$ 23.7%, i.e. about 24%.
questions.trick: Mass % Cl = (mass Cl / total mass) $\times$ 100.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which compound would give a precipitate with alcoholic AgNO$_3$ most readily at room temperature?
questions.explanation: tert-Butyl chloride ionises readily (S$_N$1, stable 3° carbocation) at room temperature to release Cl$^-$, which precipitates as AgCl; aryl and vinyl halides do not ionise due to resonance stabilisation of the C–X bond.
questions.trick: Only alkyl halides ionise readily with AgNO$_3$; 3$^\circ$ fastest via stable carbocation.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following alkyl halides would show the fastest S$_N$2 reaction with NaOH?
questions.explanation: Methyl bromide has the least steric hindrance around the electrophilic carbon, so backside attack by OH$^-$ is fastest among these.
questions.trick: Least steric hindrance wins S$_N$2: methyl halide reacts fastest.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Given pKa values: ethanol = 15.9, phenol = 10.0, p-nitrophenol = 7.15, picric acid = 0.38, the correct decreasing order of acidity is
questions.explanation: A lower pKa means a stronger acid, so ranking by increasing pKa (0.38, 7.15, 10.0, 15.9) gives decreasing acidity as picric acid > p-nitrophenol > phenol > ethanol, consistent with the number of electron-withdrawing nitro groups stabilising the phenoxide.
questions.trick: Lower pKa = stronger acid; just sort the given pKa values ascending.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following ethers would undergo the FASTEST cleavage with HI, considering steric and electronic factors?
options: Dimethyl ether (least hindered but no special stabilisation)
Di-tert-butyl ether (very hindered, but tertiary carbocation forms via S$_N$1 readily)
Methyl phenyl ether cleaving at the aryl-oxygen bond
questions.explanation: Even though di-tert-butyl ether is sterically hindered for S$_N$2, its tertiary carbon readily forms a stable carbocation, so cleavage proceeds rapidly via S$_N$1; aryl-oxygen bonds (as in anisole) do not cleave at all under these conditions.
questions.trick: Even hindered 3$^\circ$-alkyl ethers cleave fast via S$_N$1 carbocation with HI.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol?
questions.explanation: LiAlH$_4$ is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce carboxylic acids (and esters) all the way to primary alcohols; NaBH$_4$ is too weak to reduce acids.
questions.trick: LiAlH$_4$ is strong enough to reduce acids/esters all the way to 1$^\circ$ alcohol.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Neutral FeCl$_3$ solution gives a characteristic violet/blue-violet colouration with
questions.explanation: Phenols form coloured complexes with neutral FeCl$_3$ solution (typically violet/blue/green depending on the phenol), a classic qualitative test; alcohols do not give this colour.
questions.trick: Neutral FeCl$_3$ violet colour = phenol test, not alcohols.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Considering the +I effect of alkyl groups on the basicity (proton-accepting ability) of the oxygen lone pair, the correct order among ether, alcohol and water is
questions.explanation: Each alkyl group attached to oxygen donates electron density inductively, raising the electron density (and hence proton affinity) of the lone pairs on O; an ether has two alkyl groups, an alcohol has one, and water has none, giving the order ether > alcohol > water.
questions.trick: More alkyl groups on O (+I effect) = more electron-rich O = more basic: ether $>$ alcohol $>$ water.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation) is present in
questions.explanation: In salicylaldehyde, the ortho –OH and the –CHO group are close enough for the OH hydrogen to hydrogen-bond intramolecularly with the carbonyl oxygen, forming a stable six-membered ring; in the para isomer the groups are too far apart, so only intermolecular H-bonding occurs.
questions.trick: Ortho placement of OH next to C=O/COOH $\to$ intramolecular H-bond (chelation).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Compared to ethanol, ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol) has a much higher boiling point mainly because
options: ethylene glycol has a much higher boiling point because each molecule can form more intermolecular hydrogen bonds (it has two –OH groups)
ethylene glycol has a lower boiling point due to dipole cancellation
both have nearly identical boiling points since their molar masses are close
ethanol has a higher boiling point because it is a smaller molecule
questions.explanation: Each ethylene glycol molecule carries two –OH groups, so it can participate in a more extensive hydrogen-bonded network than ethanol's single –OH, requiring much more energy to separate the molecules and giving glycol a considerably higher boiling point.
questions.trick: More -OH groups per molecule = more H-bonds = much higher boiling point (glycol $>$ ethanol).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Phenol does not undergo nucleophilic substitution of the OH group easily (unlike alcohols) because
options: phenol is more acidic than alcohols
phenol has no lone pair on oxygen
the C–OH bond in phenol has partial double-bond character due to resonance with the ring
the ring destabilises the leaving hydroxide ion
questions.explanation: Conjugation of the oxygen lone pair with the ring gives the C–O bond partial double-bond character, strengthening it and making OH a poor leaving group in phenol.
questions.trick: Resonance strengthens phenol's C-O bond $\to$ OH is a poor leaving group there.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Bromine water reacts with phenol to give
questions.explanation: The OH group strongly activates and directs to o,p positions; with excess Br$_2$ water, all three available positions (2,4,6) are substituted, giving a white precipitate — used as a test for phenol.
questions.trick: Br$_2$ water + phenol $\to$ white ppt of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, classic test.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Kolbe's reaction converts sodium phenoxide into
questions.explanation: Sodium phenoxide + CO$_2$ under pressure (400 K, 4–7 atm) followed by acidification gives salicylic acid via electrophilic substitution by CO$_2$.
questions.trick: Kolbe: phenoxide + CO$_2$ (pressure) $\to$ salicylic acid after acidification.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the ceric ammonium nitrate test for the –OH group, alcohols and phenols can be distinguished because
options: alcohols give no colour while phenols turn red
both give an identical yellow colouration
alcohols give a red colouration (complex formation) while phenols give a green colouration
only tertiary alcohols react, all others give no colour
questions.explanation: Ceric ammonium nitrate reacts with the –OH group to form a coloured complex; alcohols characteristically give a red colouration, while phenols give a green colouration, allowing the two classes to be distinguished.
questions.trick: Ceric ammonium nitrate: alcohols turn red, phenols turn green — quick -OH test.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether are functional isomers because
options: they have the same molecular formula but different functional groups
one is aromatic and the other is not
questions.explanation: Both have formula C$_2$H$_6$O, but ethanol has an –OH group while dimethyl ether has a C–O–C linkage; ethanol has a much higher b.p. due to H-bonding.
questions.trick: Same formula, different functional group (OH vs C-O-C) = functional isomers.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the acidity of ethanol, water, and phenol from strongest to weakest acid?
questions.explanation: Resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion makes phenol the strongest acid of the three; ethanol is the weakest because the ethyl group's +I effect increases electron density on oxygen, disfavouring loss of H$^+$.
questions.trick: Fixed order: phenol $>$ water $>$ ethanol in acid strength.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: p-Nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol because the nitro group
options: withdraws electrons by resonance and induction, stabilising the phenoxide ion
donates electrons by resonance, stabilising phenoxide
questions.explanation: –NO$_2$ at the para position withdraws electron density through resonance and induction, delocalising the negative charge of the phenoxide ion and stabilising it, so p-nitrophenol is a stronger acid.
questions.trick: EWG (-NO$_2$) at o/p stabilises phenoxide by resonance $\to$ more acidic.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which alcohol, on oxidation with acidified K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$, gives a ketone directly?
questions.explanation: A secondary alcohol has one H on the carbinol carbon and is oxidised to a ketone; primary alcohols give aldehydes/acids, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation (no α-H).
questions.trick: 2$^\circ$ alcohol (one $\alpha$-H) oxidises to ketone; 1$^\circ$ to acid, 3$^\circ$ resists.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Williamson's synthesis of an unsymmetrical ether R–O–R' proceeds via
options: S$_N$2 attack of alkoxide ion on a primary alkyl halide
questions.explanation: Sodium alkoxide (nucleophile) attacks a primary (or methyl) alkyl halide in an S$_N$2 mechanism; a bulky/3° halide would instead undergo elimination.
questions.trick: Williamson: alkoxide + 1$^\circ$ RX via S$_N$2; 3$^\circ$ RX gives elimination instead.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol), the three –OH groups are classified as
options: one primary and two secondary OH groups
two primary OH groups and one secondary OH group
questions.explanation: Glycerol is HOCH$_2$–CHOH–CH$_2$OH; the terminal carbons (C1, C3) each bear one other carbon so their OH is primary, while the middle carbon (C2), attached to two carbons, carries a secondary OH.
questions.trick: Glycerol: end carbons give 2 primary OH, middle carbon gives 1 secondary OH.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Treating phenol with excess concentrated HNO$_3$ (with conc. H$_2$SO$_4$) gives mainly
questions.explanation: The strongly activating –OH group directs incoming NO$_2^+$ groups to the o,p positions; with excess concentrated nitrating mixture, all three available o,p positions are nitrated, giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid).
questions.trick: Phenol + excess conc. HNO$_3$/H$_2$SO$_4$ $\to$ trinitration at 2,4,6 $\to$ picric acid.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement about the industrial preparation of phenol from chlorobenzene versus from cumene is correct?
options: The Dow process (from chlorobenzene) requires much harsher conditions (623 K, 300 atm) than the more economical cumene process, which is why cumene is now the preferred industrial route
The cumene process requires extremely high pressure and temperature, unlike the Dow (chlorobenzene) process
Neither process is used industrially today
questions.explanation: The chlorobenzene route needs very high temperature and pressure due to the strong, resonance-stabilised C–Cl bond, making it energy-intensive; the cumene process operates under milder conditions and also yields useful acetone as a co-product, making it the economically preferred industrial method.
questions.trick: Cumene process is milder and gives useful acetone; Dow needs harsh 623K/300atm.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The IUPAC name of the ether CH$_3$–CH$_2$–O–CH(CH$_3$)$_2$ is
questions.explanation: The longer chain is propane, with the ethoxy (–OC$_2$H$_5$) group attached at C2 (the isopropyl carbon), giving the IUPAC name 2-ethoxypropane; 'ethyl propyl ether' is only the common (functional class) name.
questions.trick: Name ethers as alkoxy-alkane: locant of O-substituent on the parent chain.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the boiling points of alcohols compared to ethers of similar molar mass?
options: Alcohols have much lower boiling points than ethers because ethers are ionic
Ethers and alcohols of similar molar mass always boil at the same temperature
Ethers always have higher boiling points than alcohols
Alcohols have higher boiling points than ethers of comparable molar mass because alcohols can hydrogen bond with each other, while ethers cannot
questions.explanation: Alcohols possess an O–H group capable of intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which requires more energy to overcome on boiling, whereas ethers (R–O–R') have no O–H and hence weaker dipole-dipole interactions only, giving them lower boiling points.
questions.trick: O-H lets alcohols H-bond each other; ethers can't $\to$ alcohols boil higher.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Among ethanol, ethylene glycol and glycerol, the highest viscosity is shown by
options: none show any difference in viscosity
questions.explanation: Viscosity increases with the extent of intermolecular hydrogen bonding; glycerol has three –OH groups per molecule, forming the most extensive H-bonded network, making it noticeably more viscous than the diol (glycol) or the monohydric alcohol.
questions.trick: More -OH groups per molecule = more H-bonding = more viscous; glycerol $>$ glycol $>$ ethanol.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which method of alcohol preparation gives an anti-Markovnikov addition of water across a double bond?
options: Hydroboration-oxidation of an alkene (B$_2$H$_6$, then H$_2$O$_2$/NaOH)
Reduction of an aldehyde with NaBH$_4$
questions.explanation: In hydroboration-oxidation, boron adds to the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and is then replaced by OH with retention of configuration, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol; acid-catalysed hydration instead follows Markovnikov's rule.
questions.trick: Hydroboration-oxidation gives anti-Markovnikov OH; acid hydration gives Markovnikov OH.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of acidity is
questions.explanation: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance with the ring, making phenol more acidic than water, which in turn is more acidic than ethanol (no such stabilisation, +I effect of ethyl raises electron density on O).
questions.trick: Acidity: phenol $>$ water $>$ ethanol (phenoxide resonance-stabilised).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The Lucas test distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols based on
options: rate of turbidity formation with conc. HCl/ZnCl$_2$ (S$_N$1 reactivity)
questions.explanation: 3° alcohols form the more stable carbocation fastest and turn turbid immediately; 2° take a few minutes; 1° alcohols react only on heating.
questions.trick: Lucas: turbidity speed tracks carbocation stability, 3$^\circ$ instant, 1$^\circ$ on heating.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The product of Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with CH$_3$COCl/AlCl$_3$ is
questions.explanation: The acylium ion CH$_3$CO$^+$ generated from CH$_3$COCl/AlCl$_3$ substitutes onto benzene to give acetophenone (C$_6$H$_5$COCH$_3$).
questions.trick: Friedel-Crafts acylation (RCOCl/AlCl$_3$) on benzene $\to$ aryl ketone directly.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition is
questions.explanation: Fewer/smaller alkyl groups mean less +I effect and less steric hindrance at the carbonyl carbon, so formaldehyde (no alkyl group) is most reactive, then acetaldehyde, then acetone.
questions.trick: Less bulk/+I at C=O = more reactive: HCHO $>$ RCHO $>$ R$_2$CO.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following would react with acetaldehyde to form a stable, isolable bisulphite addition compound used for purification?
questions.explanation: Aldehydes and methyl ketones react with saturated sodium bisulphite (NaHSO$_3$) to form a crystalline addition compound, which can be regenerated back to the carbonyl compound with dilute acid or base — used to purify carbonyl compounds.
questions.trick: Saturated NaHSO$_3$ + aldehyde/methyl ketone $\to$ crystalline bisulphite adduct for purification.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A student wants to prepare an aldehyde from a nitrile without over-reducing it to a primary amine. Which reagent should be used?
options: DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride) at low temperature, followed by hydrolysis
questions.explanation: DIBAL-H reduces a nitrile in a controlled manner at low temperature to an imine intermediate, which on hydrolysis gives the aldehyde; LiAlH$_4$ and H$_2$/Ni over-reduce the nitrile all the way to the primary amine.
questions.trick: DIBAL-H at low temperature stops nitrile reduction exactly at the aldehyde.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Clemmensen reduction reduces a carbonyl group to CH$_2$ using
questions.explanation: Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl (acidic conditions) to reduce C=O directly to CH$_2$; Wolff-Kishner uses hydrazine/KOH (basic conditions) for the same net transformation.
questions.trick: Clemmensen = Zn-Hg/HCl (acidic); Wolff-Kishner = NH$_2$NH$_2$/KOH (basic) — same net C=O$\to$CH$_2$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Ozonolysis of 2-butene followed by reductive work-up (Zn/H$_2$O) gives
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond of CH$_3$CH=CHCH$_3$ symmetrically; reductive work-up with Zn/H$_2$O gives two molecules of acetaldehyde, each carbon of the double bond becoming a carbonyl carbon.
questions.trick: Ozonolysis splits C=C at the double bond into two carbonyls per alkene carbon.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Iodoform test (I$_2$/NaOH, yellow precipitate) is given by
questions.explanation: Compounds with a CH$_3$CO– group (acetone) or a CH$_3$CH(OH)– group (isopropanol) give the yellow CHI$_3$ precipitate on treatment with I$_2$/NaOH; formaldehyde, benzaldehyde and n-propanol lack this structural feature.
questions.trick: Iodoform needs CH$_3$CO- or CH$_3$CH(OH)-: acetone and isopropanol qualify.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which carboxylic acid derivative is most reactive towards nucleophilic acyl substitution?
questions.explanation: Acid chlorides have the best leaving group (Cl$^-$) and least electron donation into the carbonyl, making them the most electrophilic and reactive acyl derivatives; reactivity order: acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.
questions.trick: Best leaving group + least resonance donation = most reactive: acid chloride tops.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which reagent converts an aldehyde/ketone into an oxime?
questions.explanation: Hydroxylamine (NH$_2$OH) condenses with the carbonyl group, releasing water, to form an oxime (C=N–OH); this is used in the characterisation of carbonyl compounds.
questions.trick: NH$_2$OH on C=O $\to$ oxime (C=N-OH); memorise reagent-product pairs.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The correct order of acid strength is
questions.explanation: Each additional electron-withdrawing Cl atom (–I effect) further stabilises the carboxylate anion, increasing acid strength; trichloroacetic acid is the strongest.
questions.trick: More Cl (-I effect) on acid = stronger acid: Cl$_3$C $>$ Cl$_2$CH $>$ ClCH$_2$ $>$ CH$_3$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following carbonyl compounds would react with Grignard reagent to ultimately give a tertiary alcohol after work-up?
options: An ester (with 2 equivalents of Grignard reagent, giving a 3° alcohol)
questions.explanation: An ester reacts with one equivalent of RMgX to give a ketone intermediate, which reacts with a second equivalent to give, after work-up, a tertiary alcohol bearing two identical R groups from the Grignard reagent.
questions.trick: Ester + 2 RMgX $\to$ 3$^\circ$ alcohol with two identical new R groups.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Rosenmund reduction converts an acid chloride to
questions.explanation: RCOCl + H$_2$ over Pd catalyst poisoned with BaSO$_4$/quinoline stops reduction at the aldehyde stage, preventing further reduction to the alcohol.
questions.trick: Rosenmund: poisoned Pd catalyst stops RCOCl reduction exactly at RCHO.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following gives a positive Tollens' test but does not give a positive Fehling's test?
questions.explanation: Aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde reduce ammoniacal AgNO$_3$ (Tollens') to give a silver mirror, but they do not reduce Fehling's solution, which is specific to aliphatic aldehydes.
questions.trick: Aromatic aldehydes: Tollens' yes (mirror), Fehling's no — memorise this split.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Decarboxylation of sodium acetate with soda lime gives
questions.explanation: CH$_3$COONa + NaOH $\xrightarrow{\text{CaO, heat}}$ CH$_4$ + Na$_2$CO$_3$; decarboxylation removes CO$_2$ and replaces it with H.
questions.trick: Decarboxylation (soda lime) replaces -COONa with -H: acetate $\to$ methane.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A cyanohydrin is formed when a carbonyl compound reacts with
questions.explanation: HCN adds across the C=O bond (nucleophilic addition) to give an α-hydroxy nitrile, called a cyanohydrin.
questions.trick: HCN + C=O $\to$ cyanohydrin ($\alpha$-hydroxy nitrile).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which test distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone using a colour change to brick-red precipitate?
questions.explanation: Aliphatic aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution (Cu$^{2+}$ complex) to a brick-red precipitate of Cu$_2$O; ketones do not react.
questions.trick: Fehling's brick-red Cu$_2$O = aliphatic aldehydes only, not ketones.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Formic acid, unlike other carboxylic acids, reduces Tollens' reagent because
options: it is a stronger acid than other acids
it contains an aldehydic –CHO group along with –COOH
questions.explanation: HCOOH (H–COOH) structurally contains a –CHO-like hydrogen attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, giving it reducing/aldehydic character not shown by other carboxylic acids.
questions.trick: HCOOH hides a -CHO-like H $\to$ only acid that reduces Tollens'.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct statement about crossed Cannizzaro reaction?
options: It cannot occur between two different aldehydes
It occurs between two molecules of acetaldehyde only
It always gives only an alcohol as the sole product

It occurs between formaldehyde (or another aldehyde with no α-H) and an aldehyde possessing α-hydrogens, but is applied practically between two different aldehydes both lacking α-hydrogens for a clean, predictable outcome
questions.explanation: A crossed Cannizzaro reaction between two different aldehydes both lacking $\alpha$-hydrogens (e.g. formaldehyde and benzaldehyde) proceeds with a clean, predictable outcome: one is reduced to the alcohol and the other oxidised to the acid, since neither can undergo the competing aldol reaction.
questions.trick: Crossed Cannizzaro is clean only when BOTH aldehydes lack $\alpha$-hydrogens.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following acids is the strongest, based on inductive effects of the substituent?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative substituent here and withdraws electron density inductively, stabilising the carboxylate anion the most and making fluoroacetic acid the strongest acid of the four listed.
questions.trick: Most electronegative substituent (F) withdraws most $\to$ strongest acid.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which best explains why methylamine is soluble in water while N,N-dimethylaniline is much less soluble?
options: Methylamine has no nitrogen lone pair
Methylamine can hydrogen bond effectively with water and has a small alkyl group, while N,N-dimethylaniline's bulky aromatic/alkyl groups increase hydrophobic character and reduce solubility
Methylamine is ionic; N,N-dimethylaniline is covalent
questions.explanation: Small amines like methylamine hydrogen-bond effectively with water and dissolve well; as the hydrophobic (alkyl/aryl) portion of the amine grows, as in N,N-dimethylaniline, water solubility decreases sharply.
questions.trick: Bigger hydrophobic (aryl/alkyl) groups on N cut water solubility sharply.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Aniline reacts with bromine water at room temperature, without any catalyst, to give
questions.explanation: The –NH$_2$ group strongly activates the ring, so even dilute bromine water substitutes at all three available o,p positions without needing a Lewis acid catalyst, giving a white precipitate — used as a test for aniline.
questions.trick: -NH$_2$ activates so strongly, Br$_2$ water needs no catalyst: 2,4,6-tribromoaniline ppt.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol in weakly alkaline medium gives
questions.explanation: The diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and couples at the para position of phenoxide to give a coloured azo compound, the basis of azo dye chemistry.
questions.trick: Diazonium + phenol (weak base) couples at para $\to$ coloured azo dye.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Ammonolysis of ethyl bromide with excess ammonia gives predominantly
questions.explanation: Excess NH$_3$ ensures that unreacted ammonia is always in large excess relative to the forming amine, favouring monoalkylation and hence the primary amine as the major product.
questions.trick: Excess NH$_3$ in ammonolysis keeps monoalkylation favoured $\to$ mainly 1$^\circ$ amine.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following amines, when treated with excess methyl iodide followed by moist Ag$_2$O and then heated (Hofmann elimination), would be expected to give an alkene as a key step in structure elucidation?
options: A quaternary ammonium hydroxide with a $\beta$-hydrogen available, formed by exhaustive methylation of an amine
A tertiary amine with no $\beta$-hydrogens at all
questions.explanation: Exhaustive methylation of an amine gives a quaternary ammonium salt; converting it to the hydroxide and heating causes Hofmann elimination, in which a $\beta$-hydrogen is removed along with the trialkylamine leaving group to give an alkene (historically used to determine amine structure).
questions.trick: Exhaustive methylation to quaternary hydroxide + heat + $\beta$-H $\to$ Hofmann elimination.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is the major organic product when aniline reacts with acetic anhydride?
questions.explanation: The nucleophilic nitrogen of aniline attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetic anhydride, displacing acetate, to give acetanilide (C$_6$H$_5$NHCOCH$_3$) as the major product.
questions.trick: Aniline's N attacks acetic anhydride's carbonyl $\to$ acetanilide, displacing acetate.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following correctly gives the product of the reaction between an aryl diazonium salt and hypophosphorous acid (H$_3$PO$_2$)/water?
options: The diazonium group is replaced by iodine
The diazonium group is replaced by hydrogen (deamination), regenerating the parent arene
questions.explanation: H$_3$PO$_2$ is a mild reducing agent that replaces the diazonium (–N$_2^+$) group with hydrogen, releasing N$_2$ gas — a useful method for removing an amino group from an aromatic ring after it has served its purpose in directing earlier substitutions (deamination).
questions.trick: H$_3$PO$_2$/H$_2$O on diazonium = deamination: -N$_2^+$ replaced by H.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The Hofmann bromamide reaction of benzamide (C$_6$H$_5$CONH$_2$) with Br$_2$/NaOH gives
options: aniline (C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$, one carbon fewer than the amide)
questions.explanation: Hofmann degradation removes the carbonyl carbon as CO$_2$ (via an isocyanate intermediate), so benzamide (C$_6$H$_5$CONH$_2$) gives aniline (C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$), which has one carbon less than benzamide.
questions.trick: Hofmann on benzamide drops the carbonyl carbon $\to$ gives aniline, not benzylamine.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the Hinsberg test, a secondary amine reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to give a product that is
options: insoluble in KOH (and has no acidic N–H)
insoluble in the reaction mixture but soluble in KOH
questions.explanation: A secondary amine forms an N,N-disubstituted sulphonamide with no N–H hydrogen left to ionise, so it remains insoluble even after adding KOH; a primary amine's sulphonamide retains one acidic N–H and dissolves in KOH.
questions.trick: Hinsberg: 2$^\circ$ amine's sulphonamide has no N-H $\to$ stays insoluble in KOH.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used to prepare
options: aromatic amines directly from aryl halides
questions.explanation: Phthalimide's potassium salt undergoes S$_N$2 with an alkyl halide, and hydrolysis releases a pure primary amine, free of secondary/tertiary contamination; aryl halides do not undergo S$_N$2, so this method fails for aromatic amines.
questions.trick: Gabriel synthesis gives pure 1$^\circ$ aliphatic amine only; fails for aryl halides.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of these tests can be used to distinguish a secondary amine from both primary and tertiary amines?
options: Solubility in water (all are similarly soluble for small amines)
Reaction with dilute HCl (all amines react)
Reaction with HNO$_2$: secondary amines uniquely give a yellow oily N-nitrosoamine
questions.explanation: With cold HNO$_2$, primary aliphatic amines evolve N$_2$ gas (with an alcohol), secondary amines give a characteristic yellow oily nitrosoamine, and tertiary amines give no clean reaction (only an unstable salt), so the nitrosoamine formation uniquely identifies secondary amines.
questions.trick: Only 2$^\circ$ amines give the unique yellow N-nitrosoamine with HNO$_2$.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A primary aliphatic amine reacts with HNO$_2$ (NaNO$_2$/HCl, cold) to give
options: an alcohol with brisk evolution of N$_2$ gas
questions.explanation: Aliphatic diazonium salts are highly unstable even at 0–5°C and decompose immediately, releasing N$_2$ gas and forming the corresponding alcohol via a carbocation intermediate.
questions.trick: 1$^\circ$ aliphatic amine + HNO$_2$ $\to$ brisk N$_2$ gas + alcohol (unstable diazonium).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct laboratory distinguishing test to confirm a compound is a primary amine and NOT a secondary or tertiary amine?
options: It reacts with NaOH to give a precipitate
It gives a foul-smelling isocyanide with CHCl$_3$/alcoholic KOH, AND its benzenesulphonamide derivative dissolves in KOH (soluble sulphonamide due to acidic N–H)
questions.explanation: Both the positive carbylamine test and the Hinsberg test result (soluble sulphonamide, since one acidic N–H remains) are diagnostic specifically for primary amines, distinguishing them from secondary (insoluble sulphonamide, no carbylamine) and tertiary (no reaction in either test) amines.
questions.trick: 1$^\circ$-only signature: positive carbylamine AND KOH-soluble sulphonamide together.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The secondary structure of a protein (α-helix, β-pleated sheet) is mainly stabilised by
options: hydrogen bonding between C=O and N–H groups of the peptide backbone
questions.explanation: Regular H-bonding patterns between the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of the polypeptide backbone hold the chain in a helix or sheet arrangement.
questions.trick: Secondary structure = H-bonds between backbone C=O and N-H, not side chains.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement about DNA and RNA structure is correct?
options: DNA is usually single-stranded; RNA is double-stranded
DNA is usually double-stranded (helix); RNA is usually single-stranded
questions.explanation: DNA exists as a double helix of two complementary strands, whereas RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) is typically a single strand that may fold on itself.
questions.trick: DNA = double helix; RNA = usually single-stranded — fixed rule.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: In the DNA double helix, adenine pairs with thymine through
options: no hydrogen bonds, only van der Waals forces
questions.explanation: A=T pairing involves two hydrogen bonds, while G≡C pairing involves three, making G-C rich regions of DNA more thermally stable.
questions.trick: A=T two H-bonds; G$\equiv$C three H-bonds — GC-rich DNA is more stable.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Cellulose differs from starch mainly in that cellulose has
options: β-1,4 glycosidic linkages, making it indigestible by humans
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a linear polymer of glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; human digestive enzymes can hydrolyse only α-linkages (as in starch), so cellulose passes through undigested (roughage).
questions.trick: $\beta$-1,4 links in cellulose can't be cleaved by human (only $\alpha$-) enzymes.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Vitamins that must be supplied regularly in the diet because they cannot be stored in the body are
questions.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, C) are excreted in urine and not stored appreciably, so regular dietary intake is required, unlike fat-soluble vitamins which are stored in adipose tissue and liver.
questions.trick: Water-soluble vitamins (B, C) aren't stored $\to$ need daily diet supply.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The cyclic (pyranose) structure of glucose best explains
options: the absence of Schiff's test and the existence of two anomeric (α and β) forms
questions.explanation: In the cyclic hemiacetal form the aldehyde carbon becomes a new stereocentre (anomeric carbon), giving α and β anomers, and glucose fails to give the Schiff's test because the free aldehyde group is masked in the ring.
questions.trick: Cyclic hemiacetal masks -CHO $\to$ no Schiff's test, but gives $\alpha$/$\beta$ anomers.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of these statements about enzyme specificity is correct?
options: Enzymes catalyse a wide range of unrelated reactions with equal efficiency
Enzymes work equally well at all temperatures and pH values
Enzymes generally catalyse one specific reaction or a closely related set of reactions, based on the complementary shape of their active site to the substrate (lock-and-key or induced-fit model)
questions.explanation: Enzymes are highly specific because their active site has a particular 3-D shape and chemical environment that matches (or adapts to, in induced fit) only certain substrates; extreme pH or temperature denatures the enzyme and destroys this specificity.
questions.trick: Enzyme specificity = active site shape matches substrate (lock-key/induced fit).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes an increase in blood clotting time?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is essential for the synthesis of clotting factors (prothrombin); its deficiency increases blood clotting time and causes excessive bleeding.
questions.trick: Vitamin K deficiency $\to$ increased blood clotting time (needed for prothrombin).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with beri-beri, characterised by nerve and cardiovascular problems?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B$_1$ (thiamine) deficiency leads to beri-beri, which affects the nervous and cardiovascular systems.
questions.trick: B$_1$ (thiamine) deficiency = beri-beri, nerve/cardiovascular symptoms.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists a key structural difference between DNA and RNA regarding their sugar component?
options: Both contain identical sugars with no difference
DNA contains 2-deoxyribose (lacking an OH at C2'); RNA contains ribose (with an OH at C2')
Neither DNA nor RNA contains a sugar component
questions.explanation: DNA's sugar, 2-deoxyribose, lacks the hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon present in RNA's sugar, ribose; this structural difference contributes to DNA's greater chemical stability, suited to long-term genetic storage.
questions.trick: DNA sugar lacks 2'-OH (deoxyribose); RNA sugar keeps it (ribose).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which linkage type makes cellulose resistant to digestion by human digestive enzymes?
options: $\beta$-1,4 glycosidic linkage (human enzymes can only cleave $\alpha$-linkages)
questions.explanation: Human digestive enzymes (amylases) can hydrolyse only $\alpha$-glycosidic linkages (as in starch); cellulose's $\beta$-1,4 linkages cannot be cleaved by these enzymes, so cellulose acts as roughage rather than a nutrient in humans.
questions.trick: Human enzymes cleave only $\alpha$-links; cellulose's $\beta$-1,4 resists digestion.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which pair of vitamins are correctly classified as fat-soluble, capable of being stored in the body's adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and can be stored in the liver and adipose tissue, unlike water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, C), which must be regularly supplied in the diet since excess is excreted.
questions.trick: Fat-soluble, stored vitamins: A, D, E, K — remember 'ADEK'.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: A nucleoside consists of
options: a nitrogenous base + a pentose sugar
questions.explanation: A nucleoside is base + sugar (no phosphate); adding a phosphate group gives a nucleotide, the repeating unit of nucleic acid polymers.
questions.trick: Nucleoside = base + sugar; add phosphate to get a nucleotide.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which level of protein structure describes the actual three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain, stabilised by interactions such as hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges, and hydrophobic interactions among side chains?
questions.explanation: Tertiary structure refers to the overall 3-D folding of a single polypeptide chain, held together by various non-covalent interactions and disulphide bonds between distant amino acid side chains, giving the protein its unique functional shape.
questions.trick: Tertiary structure = single chain's full 3-D fold (H-bonds, S-S, hydrophobic).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares nucleosides and nucleotides?
options: A nucleoside is base + sugar + phosphate; a nucleotide is base + sugar only
A nucleoside and a nucleotide are identical in composition
A nucleoside is base + sugar; a nucleotide additionally has a phosphate group esterified to the sugar
questions.explanation: A nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous base linked to a pentose sugar; when a phosphate group is attached to the sugar (typically at the 5' position), the resulting unit is called a nucleotide, the monomer of nucleic acids.
questions.trick: Nucleoside = base+sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate ester.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: The peptide bond linking two amino acids is formed by
options: an addition reaction between two –COOH groups
a substitution reaction between two –NH$_2$ groups
a condensation reaction between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH$_2$ of another, releasing water
questions.explanation: The peptide (amide) bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next, eliminating a molecule of water.
questions.trick: Peptide bond: -COOH + -NH$_2$ condense, releasing H$_2$O, forming -CO-NH-.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which functional role does m-RNA play in protein synthesis?
options: It supplies energy for peptide bond formation
It stores the genetic code permanently in the nucleus
It carries the genetic code copied from DNA to the ribosome to direct amino acid sequence during protein synthesis
It forms the double helix with DNA
questions.explanation: Messenger RNA (m-RNA) is synthesised as a complementary copy of a DNA gene (transcription) and carries this genetic information to ribosomes, where it directs the sequence of amino acids added during translation (protein synthesis).
questions.trick: mRNA copies DNA's code and carries it to ribosomes for translation.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which functional group is common to both glucose and fructose, and which distinguishes them structurally?
options: Glucose has no OH groups; fructose has five
Both are aldoses; they differ only in ring size
Glucose is an aldohexose (has –CHO); fructose is a ketohexose (has C=O at C2); both have the molecular formula C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$
questions.explanation: Glucose and fructose are structural (functional) isomers with the same molecular formula, C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$, but glucose has an aldehyde group (aldohexose) while fructose has a ketone group at C-2 (ketohexose).
questions.trick: Glucose = aldohexose (-CHO); fructose = ketohexose (C=O at C2); same formula.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the isoelectric point of an amino acid?
options: The pH at which the amino acid is fully positively charged
The pH at which the amino acid is fully negatively charged
The pH at which the amino acid exists predominantly as the zwitterion with no net charge, and hence shows minimum solubility and does not migrate in an electric field
The temperature at which the amino acid decomposes
questions.explanation: At the isoelectric point, the amino acid exists as a neutral dipolar zwitterion (equal positive and negative charge), has minimum solubility, and does not move towards either electrode in an electric field (used in electrophoretic separation).
questions.trick: Isoelectric point: zwitterion, net charge zero, minimum solubility, no migration.
questions.subject: chemistry
